title: Coach who sent teen 'inappropriate' messages banned from working with kids
text:
An Adelaide sports coach has been banned from working with children after a tribunal found he sent inappropriate messages to a teenager.

The man was acquitted of a charge of communicating to make a child amenable to sexual activity in the South Australian District Court last year because the alleged offence had not been proven beyond reasonable doubt.

But the Department of Human Services issued a notice prohibiting the man from engaging in child-related work.

The man sought a review of the department's decision, which has been upheld by the South Australian Civil and Administrative Tribunal.

In a recently published decision, the tribunal found the man sent the teenager more than 140 Facebook messages over a four-month period, which "demonstrate[d] an inappropriate and overly familiar pattern of communication".

"The messages indicate that the applicant initiated and continued the contact, persisting even after the child asked the applicant to stop," the ruling stated.

"Although there is no explicit sexual content in the Facebook conversations, the applicant's messages show a complete lack of boundaries and a secret nature to their relationship.

"In my view, the Facebook messages by themselves are enough for me to find the applicant poses an unacceptable risk of harm to children."

The South Australian Civil and Administrative Tribunal upheld the Department of Human Services's decision to prohibit the man from working with children. (ABC News: Eugene Boisvert)

The tribunal found the coach made "a series of lapses of judgement", which included communicating with the child via Facebook, requesting the child's Snapchat details and an occasion where he called the child at 10pm.

The man did not deny the Facebook communication and accepted it was "inappropriate", the tribunal heard.

The tribunal noted the man had also previously been found guilty of a dishonesty offence which, along with the unproven allegation of other sexual communications with the child, necessitated "a conclusion that he is an unacceptable risk of harm to children".

The tribunal agreed with the department that the man's conduct was "a serious breach of professional boundaries" and that the messages were "indicative of grooming behaviour".

It said child safety laws required the safety and protection of children must be the paramount consideration.

"This scheme is not about punishing the applicant however it is a privilege and not a right to work with children," the ruling stated.

"At this point in time, I consider that if the applicant were permitted to work with children, this would not ensure the adequate protection of children."

title: Woman loses legal battle over roof painted 'disturbing' shade of red
text:
A woman has been ordered to repaint her roof by a Queensland tribunal after neighbours complained the colour was "offensive", "disturbing," and "threatening".

The Queensland Civil and Administrative Tribunal (QCAT) handed down its ruling today, following a three-year-long dispute between Maria Gourley and her body corporate.

It comes after Maria Gourley painted her roof "heritage red" instead of "Nutech coral" at her townhouse at The Gap, in March 2023.

The Fernbrook townhouse complex runs under a community titles scheme. (ABC Radio Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

The Fernbrook body corporate took Ms Gourley to the Office of the Commissioner for Body Corporate and Community Management for adjudication.

The adjudicator ruled the body corporate's order to repaint the roof was "reasonable" because the colour was "glaringly" different to the other houses.

Ms Gourley appealed the decision in QCAT, but on Monday afternoon tribunal senior member Richard Oliver upheld the adjudicator's previous ruling.

"The question of reasonableness is a little tricky; it's not what I think is reasonable or what you think is reasonable," Mr Oliver said.

"The adjudicator's job is to determine whether or not the body corporate's decision is reasonable.

"It's fairly clear this conclusion, about it being quite different to the remainder of the roofs in the complex, is a reasonable conclusion of fact to come to, because it's obvious."

Fernbrook body corporate committee member Jill Elsworth told the tribunal that the roof disturbed the visual harmony of the neighbourhood.

"Maria's was a totally contrasting, discordant colour," Ms Elsworth said.

Mr Oliver threw out her appeal, ordering her to repaint her roof Nutech coral at her own expense within the next three months.

Speaking outside the tribunal, Ms Gourley told 612 ABC she was disappointed by the verdict.

"I still don't think this is right," Ms Gourley said.

"I'm going home to explore my options and go from there."

A neighbourhood in uproar

Ms Gourley asked the body corporate what colour she should paint her roof in January 2023.

However, the body corporate did not have a specific colour in its bylaws, instead telling Ms Gourley to choose shades that were similar to other roofs.

Neighbours told the adjudicator the roof was "jarring", "disruptive", and "alien". (ABC Radio Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

The colour Nutech coral was chosen retrospectively in October 2023, following complaints from neighbours when Ms Gourley painted her roof heritage red.

612 ABC has obtained copies of the submissions sent to the adjudicator complaining about the colour of Ms Gourley's roof.

"It is an offensive colour and indicates that the committee is not implementing the bylaws." - Jill Elsworth "M. Gourley's painting of her roof in a bright red colour from first glance appears a blatant act of defiance against the committee. It is my opinion that M.Gourley's action poses a disregard of, even a threat to others' investment. - Janine Begg "It would appear that the owner of lot 62 has flouted the bylaws and seems determined to upset the entire complex, especially those residents who have to look at her jarringly coloured roof each and every day." - Michael and Julia Murphy

Ms Gourley said none of the neighbours had ever knocked on her door to complain about the roof in person.

The Fernbrook body corporate declined to comment.

title: Veggie-packed side dishes that are worthy of the main course
text:
When is a side dish not a side? When it's promoted to the main course.

From a Nepalese-style dal bhat and mushroomy French toast to loaded sweet potatoes and whole roasted cauliflower, these recipes make for simple, satisfying and nutritious midweek dinners in their own right.

Dhal is the ultimate budget food and this lightly-spiced version is warm, comforting and perfect served with steamed rice and pickles or chutney (ABC News: Nip Liyanapathirana)

Dal often plays second fiddle to other dishes as part of a banquet, but this dal bhat from Sydney-based chef Nip Liyanapathirana is more than worthy of being the main event.

It's a simple and nourishing dish comprised of split red lentils and a few spices, but with its own Nepalese-style character from the mustard oil and the crispy tarka poured over the top.

Including prep time, it's ready in 40 minutes and is best served with steamed rice and any South Asian pickles or chutney.

This French toast with earthy mushrooms, parmesan, and a touch of crème fraîche is the perfect savoury bite and an easy option for weeknight dinners. (ABC TV: Wesley Mitton)

Alice Zaslavsky whipped up this savoury spin on French toast for Brian Nankervis on season two of A Bite to Eat With Alice.

The buttery, golden French toast base is rich, comforting and full of depth and it's topped with a delicious and creamy mix of caramelised mushrooms, Dijon mustard, crème fraiche, fresh herbs and a hint of lemon.

A loaded sweet potato with creamy mushroom, chicken with grated cheese on top ready to grill. (ABC News: Zain Ayub)

Sweet potatoes are in season and in plentiful supply and this recipe by Ismat Awan is an excellent way to put them to good use.

The roasted sweet potatoes are stuffed with a parsley-forward creamy mushroom and chicken filling and finished with a grated sharp cheddar and cracked black pepper.

Whether you serve it solo or pair it a crunchy salad, it'll be sure to become a part of regular rotation.

A whole cauliflower is brushed with a spice oil before it is wrapped and roasted. A delicious vegetarian side. (ABC News: Lina Jebeile)

This whole roasted cauliflower recipe from Jina Jebeile uses simple ingredients, but it's packed with flavour and oozing with melted, gooey cheese.

Simply brush the whole cauliflower with spiced garlic and herb oil, place it on top of sliced red onions and roast until tender. Before serving, it's topped with a good handful of cheese and roasted again.

The end result is a beautifully caramelised cauliflower with crispy, cheesy edges and soft, flavourful florets.

title: Big is beautiful as Australia's first UFC champion finally comes home
text:
It has taken more than a decade, but Rob Whittaker, Australia's first-ever UFC champion, is finally coming home.

The UFC light-heavyweight has been confirmed for the promotion's next card in Sydney on February 7, where he will face Uzbekistan's Bogdan Guskov in his first hometown fight in over 12 years.

Whittaker can barely recall his last effort in the Harbour City, when he knocked out American Clint Hester in 2014.

It came so early in his career it was closer to his Padstow products days as a Railcorp electrician than a world champion.

"It's hard to remember, to be honest. So much has happened since. I've ridden the rollercoaster," said Whittaker.

Rob Whittaker last fought in Sydney in 2014. (Getty Images via Zuffa LLC: Josh Hedges )

"My friends and family can all be there. They can be a part of the whole journey without having to spend a billion bucks to be there.

"But I hope things settle down. I'm going to have to stop replying (to people asking for tickets).

"It'll be good to be home after so long. You normally have to travel so far to put on a show."

Putting on a show far and wide has been second nature for Whittaker during his long career with the UFC.

Since that night in Sydney, all but one of his UFC losses have come against future or reigning world champions, confirming his status as one of Australia's top combat sport exports.

The 35-year-old snuck in a few fights on home soil, but the last was in 2019 when he lost the middleweight title against Israel Adesanya in Melbourne in front of over 57,000 fans, still the biggest crowd in UFC history.

The crowd won't quite be the same at the Sydney SuperDome for this card, headlined by rising Perth lightweight Quillin Salkilld's bout with Benoit St Denis, but Whittaker — a father of three sons and three daughters — is just happy he can take his kids to work.

Rob Whittaker recently broke a two-fight losing streak. (Getty Images via Zuffa LLC: Ed Mulholland )

"Last fight, my two eldest could come. This time it might be my three eldest. They loved it last time, and I loved having them be a part of it," said Whittaker.

"They get to see their old man work for a living. I'm sure half the time they think I'm unemployed.

"I love fighting. I don't think there's a cooler way to earn money if we want to keep it real basic, and I'm good at it as well. I'm earning a trade, and I'm going to keep doing it."

The fight will be Whittaker's second since moving from middleweight (83.91kg) to light-heavyweight (92.99kg).

After a third-round knockout win in his division debut over Nikita Krylov in July, he has plenty of confidence after snapping a two-fight losing streak.

Whittaker was wary of the power difference against bigger fighters, but after a strong start, where he left Krylov with a broken jaw, bigger has become beautiful.

Rob Whittaker has bulked up from middleweight to light-heavyweight. (Getty Images via Zuffa LLC: Ed Mulholland )

"I'm definitely more confident in my ability to zip and zag and my ability to land power, to be faster, to have the confidence to shoot when I feel it, to have confidence in my instincts again," said Whittaker.

"I can eat for fuel, I don't need to starve myself, and that makes living — especially with a family and heaps of kids — much more enjoyable.

"But it's a slippery slope, because after a fight I can get really stuck in.

"Light-heavyweight eating is different to middleweight eating, let me tell you."

Guskov has a strong track record with 15 knockouts from his 18 wins, but Whittaker is confident he has the experience to outpoint the 34-year-old.

"He's a big, rangy guy. He hits hard, he's finished a lot of people, but there's nothing he brings to the table that I haven't seen in my years in the game," said Whittaker.

"There's nothing he brings to the table I think I can't beat."

title: Food stall pops up at Big Splash in bid to comply with lease
text:
Access Canberra says it's "more likely than not" a pop-up food stall that appeared at Big Splash water park on Sunday meets the site's lease requirements for an "unlicensed family restaurant".

The site's operator had until November 1 to comply with the lease by operating either an aquatic facility, indoor sports facility or a family restaurant on the derelict Macquarie site.

Yesterday, a food stall appeared out the front of the site consisting of a portable gazebo and a barbecue, along with plastic chairs and tables, and a portaloo.

The pop-up food stall included a portable gazebo, a barbeque and a portaloo. (ABC News: Grace O'Dea)

"I don't think anyone would accept that what was here yesterday — as lovely as the people were and as nice as the watermelon drink that I had was — was an unlicensed family restaurant," Canberra Liberals MLA Peter Cain said on 666 ABC Radio Canberra.

" Even if at the extremity of believability it was an unlicensed family restaurant, it's not here today, and my understanding is, it won't be. "

But Head of Access Canberra Josh Rynehart said the regulator had considered a range of factors and are "satisfied that on the balance of probabilities it is more likely than not that this lease is compliant".

Head of Access Canberra Josh Rynehart says it is more likely than not that the lease is compliant (ABC News: David Sciasci)

"This includes consideration of the wording within the lease which could be classed as permissive — meaning that it permits activity but doesn't necessarily require that activity to be undertaken," Mr Rynehart said.

" A number of activities, including the wording within the lease and the works that have been undertaken over the last few months to replace the fencing, are all factors we have considered. "

'Unlicensed family restaurant' an undefined term

In a statement, Access Canberra said the Crown lease "does not define the term 'unlicensed family restaurant' or prescribe a particular building type, operating model, scale or minimum frequency of operation".

"We recognise that this outcome may not meet the expectations of members of the community who want to see Big Splash restored as a water park," it said.

"However, the role of the regulator is to apply the law as it stands, based on the facts and circumstances of each individual matter.

" Regulatory action cannot be taken simply because a different outcome may be preferred and where there are not reasonable prospects of success of litigation. "

Access Canberra had previously suggested that a temporary way for the operator to meet leasing conditions could be to put a food van on the site.

Canberra's only water park has been closed since the beginning of 2024. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Attorney-General Tara Cheyne acknowledged the community's disappointment this morning on 666 ABC Radio Canberra.

"Did people want to see a tent? No," she said.

" But does that mean that they're not complying with the lease or they're not genuine about wanting to meet the requirements under the lease so that it can be sold as a going concern? That's a different question. "

Many locals are frustrated that Big Splash has not reopened as a water park this year. (ABC News: Grace O'Dea)

Calls for the government to take tougher action

Big Splash, which was a privately owned and operated business, has been closed for more than two years, and was put up for sale in June.

Translink Management Group bought the lease in 2021 for $7.5 million.

The site is currently being run by a small financial firm in Sydney that loaned Translink Management Group the money to purchase the lease.

There was no pop-up food stall at the Big Splash site on Monday. (ABC News: Grace O'Dea)

While there has long been a push for the government to purchase, restore and publicly run the park, the government has said its strong preference is for the park to remain privately operated.

But Save Big Splash's Mark Pickering said it was time Planning Minister Chris Steel stepped in to "do what needs to be done".

Big Splash water park is currently derelict. (ABC News)

"Certainly under the lease, the leaseholder is required to maintain the site. Is the site maintained? Certainly not," he said.

"If the site is not maintained, [the] government can step in and maintain the site at the cost of the leaseholder.

" Why has government not done that? Why has it been allowed to fall into the level of disrepair that it is in? "

Jo Clay says she doesn't think a "tent and a table" constitutes an "unlicensed family restaurant". (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Greens MLA Jo Clay suggested there were "are at least three different ways the government could take the lease back".

"They could acquire it, they could buy it, or they could terminate it," she said on 666 ABC Radio Canberra.

" And if the minister doesn't have the legislation needed to enforce this site, the minister has the ability to change the legislation. He's got a pretty willing parliament at the moment. "

Cheyne: A 'really tricky site to deal with'

The government committed to a "comprehensive options analysis" to determine Big Splash 's future in September.

But Ms Cheyne said it was a "really tricky site" to deal with, and she defended Access Canberra's actions so far.

Tara Cheyne says the government is yet to value the site. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

"No regulator, no government can rewrite the Crown lease," she said.

"We're operating on what the Crown lease says. That purpose clause was written decades ago.

" It's done its job pretty badly, and that's what needs fixing. "

Ms Cheyne also said that terminating the lease would be difficult, and the government was yet to do a valuation of the site.

Big Splash is a privately owned and operated business, and was put up for sale in June. (ABC News: Monte Bovill)

"The Self-Government Act says we can't acquire property without just terms, and our own compensation clause probably doesn't get us there," she said.

"Those termination provisions probably need fixing."

Access Canberra says it will continue to monitor the site and "take further regulatory action if circumstances arise that warrant it".

title: Australian batting 'stronger' despite repeat South Africa collapses
text:
Coach Andrew McDonald says Australia's batting is in a better place now than before the South Africa tour, despite admitting the team underperformed in the 2-1 series loss.

Players began flying out of South Africa on Sunday and Monday, with Australia to now turn its focus to a home series against New Zealand and a tour of India that starts in January.

There remains an ongoing sense of frustration about the way the South Africa tour ended, with McDonald lamenting several missed opportunities to clinch the series.

That includes letting South Africa off the hook with the ball in Gqeberha and Cape Town, while nightmare collapses in both those Tests also hurt.

Australia has been 4-95 or worse in 14 of its past 25 Test innings, with that brittleness exposed again as the team slumped to 8-62 on the series-deciding day five in Cape Town.

But Australia's coach pointed to the performances of Cameron Green, Matt Renshaw and Josh Inglis as reasons for legitimate positivity, with the latter two scoring centuries.

Josh Inglis scored a superb century in Cape Town. (Getty Images: Grant Pitcher/Gallo Images)

"If you look at the batting unit, I think we walk away in a stronger position," McDonald said.

"For Josh Inglis to step up at late notice [in Cape Town] … he's been a batter that's been carried around with us for a while; it's exciting.

"Albeit there's a lot of negativity floating around at the moment, it's exciting to see him and Cameron Green and even Matthew Renshaw."

McDonald also admitted selectors would have some decisions to make "around the age profile of that team", with 23-year-old Cooper Connolly playing his second Test in Cape Town and Sam Konstas firing in the Sheffield Shield.

Selections and strategy in the spotlight After a disastrous series loss to South Africa, Australian cricket faces some tough decisions.

"It's still a very good cricket team with a lot of very good players in there, and down the path they will be acknowledged as legends of the game," McDonald said of the current side.

"So we've got to balance that out with who comes in, what the next decisions are.''

Beyond the obvious turning points, McDonald pointed to Australia's inability to build a big first-innings lead in Cape Town after starting day three at close to parity with four wickets down as a big moment in the series.

But he stressed that not all fault lay with the batters, after the bowlers failed to put a final nail in South Africa on day four in Cape Town.

Australia has now lost three of its past five Tests, with the back-to-back defeats in Gqeberha and Cape Town the first successive failures since the 2023 Border-Gavaskar Trophy.

The defeats have cost Australia the number one spot in the rankings, ahead of a nine-month period that includes the away Border-Gavaskar Trophy and Ashes series.

Still, McDonald pointed to Pat Cummins's 60 per cent win rate as skipper and the fact it was one of the highest among all Australian captains.

"We've underachieved here," McDonald said.

"It feels as though it's hard to win on the road. That's the greatest challenge, and that's where we will be critiqued.

"And we're incredibly frustrated that we weren't able to execute this tour after being 1-0 up."

AAP

title: West Coast Eagles star suffers brutal injury news
text:
West Coast could be without midfielder Ella Roberts for the entire 2027 AFLW season after scans confirmed the superstar had ruptured her anterior cruciate ligament (ACL).

Roberts, 21, suffered the right knee injury when she planted her leg in an attempt to change direction in the first quarter of Saturday's loss to Hawthorn, the Eagles' final game of the campaign after failing to make finals.

The midfielder immediately went down and had to be assisted from the field.

The Eagles confirmed on Monday that Roberts had torn her ACL and would need a knee reconstruction.

Given the typical 12-month recovery from that surgery, Roberts will be racing the clock to feature at all next year.

"We are all saddened by the injury sustained by Ella," West Coast AFLW boss Michelle Cowan said.

"Our priority is to arrange surgery as soon as possible and ensure she receives the very best care and we will wrap our arms around her throughout this journey.

"She is a true professional and we have every confidence she will approach her recovery with the same diligence and determination, fully supported by our medical team."

Roberts, who can play both midfield and forward, is one of the most talented players in the game and has kicked 20 goals in 55 games since her 2022 debut.

She is a two-time All-Australian and won the Eagles' best and fairest award in 2024 and 2025.

Roberts averaged 21.7 disposals and five clearances this year as West Coast finished 13th.

AAP

title: Albanese to discuss rule change for British backpackers
text:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will discuss tightening the rules for British backpacker visas when he meets with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham in the Caribbean this week.

Currently, the UK free trade deal allows British backpackers to stay in Australia for up to three years without requiring specific work to be undertaken.

However, other Working Holiday Maker visa holders must work in regional and rural areas if they wish to extend their visas beyond a year.

That arrangement has seen a sharp rise in UK backpackers, from about 47,000 in 2024 to nearly 80,000 last financial year, according to Home Affairs data.

But with the government under political pressure to lower its net overseas migration numbers, Mr Albanese is set to seek a change to the rules for UK citizens when he meets Mr Burnham at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda.

The discussions mark a departure from Mr Albanese's previous position, when he told the ABC in August that there would be no changes to the deal that exempts British backpackers from regional work rules.

Mr Albanese flagged last week that he would be bringing up the issue with Mr Burnham.

"Those UK backpackers are arriving in very large numbers … and they are staying at Bondi Beach or Coogee or around particularly the capital cities and working in hospitality there," Mr Albanese said.

"That's placing enormous pressure because it's distorting the labour market in these areas as well.

"That's just one of the areas in which we'll put forward changes. That requires discussions, and I'll be meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham."

Backpacker back-and-forth

The Coalition and One Nation have repeatedly advocated for backpacking visas to survive migration cuts, saying they are a vital resource in their regional electorates.

The National Farmers' Federation (NFF) has also stressed the backpacking workforce is essential for the agriculture sector.

Backpackers are an essential workforce for fruit harvesting. (Supplied: Milan Scheunemann)

In August, Home Affairs quietly slowed the processing of working holiday visas, sparking concerns about workforce shortages in the regions.

In September, the NFF made an emergency deal with the government to fast-track urgent visa requests for backpacker workers in harvest and fruit-picking.

Under changes proposed by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke at the National Press Club in September, a ballot and cap system would be introduced.

For backpackers hoping to stay on for a second year, places would be capped at 45,000 and they would need to undertake 88 days of regional work to enter the ballot.

Third-year spots would be capped at 5,000 places with a six-month regional work requirement.

NFF head Michael Guerin welcomed the prime minister's discussions, but said the issue of worker shortages in the agriculture sector was broader than the UK deal, pointing to a slowing of visa processing and a proposed cap and ballot system for backpackers.

"[It's] a step in the right direction, but not dealing with the fundamental underlying issue," he said.

"We have a crisis point in Australia, based on the inability to get a hold of the workforce we need to guarantee that food security we've taken for granted for generations.

"One in seven of our workers to harvest our food, keep our supermarket shelves filled, come from overseas."

Angus Taylor has dismissed the idea of a ballot for backpacker visa extensions. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

Opposition leader Angus Taylor said Mr Albanese's "outsourcing" of the issue to his UK counterpart was "desperate", despite highlighting that the Coalition's position was to encourage more backpackers to go regional.

"This is a desperate prime minister who's not only lost control of the economy, he's lost control of our borders," Mr Taylor said.

"We want them doing rural and regional work. That's a centrepiece of our policy.

"But what Labor's proposing is a ballot for who gets to stay; it's a raffle. I mean, seriously, pick the people who are going to contribute in the places where we need them."

Nationals leader Matt Canavan said the Coalition had a "completely elegant solution" and would put a fee in place for any backpacker wanting to stay in Australia for a second or third year working in a capital city.

"We would impose a fee on that, and that fee would help encourage people to get back to the regional work," he said.

title: Quick hits: NZ duo on brink of history as Lebanon goes into folklore
text:
The group stage of the Rugby League World Cup is in the books after a remarkable double-header to finish things off.

Lebanon's golden-point win over France and Tonga and Samoa's epic showdown were both classics, giving the tournament the close finishes that have been in short supply.

With Australia, New Zealand, Tonga and Samoa progressing to the semifinals, here are the quick hits from the final round of matches.

1. Was this the last World Cup for the old Kumuls?

Gairo Voro is one of several Papua New Guinea players with a big future. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

No country in rugby league will see the sport transform in their nation from this World Cup to the next like Papua New Guinea.

The entry of the PNG Chiefs to the NRL in 2028, with their near-limitless resources and game-bending salary cap concessions, will change the game in the land where they love it most.

So long as the Chiefs fulfil their promise of creating strong pathways for local talent to make it to the top level, it has the potential to change the national side forever.

England's World Cup fate is resting on a miracle After a scratchy win over Papua New Guinea, England's Rugby League World Cup needs a miracle to stay alive.

The prospect of talents like five-eighth Gairo Voro, who scored a sharp solo try, or winger Dudley Dutoi, who got the better of England star Dom Young, getting regular NRL football is a tantalising one.

The two were among Papua New Guinea's best in a spirited defeat, and from the Highlands to the islands of New Britain there can be so many more like them.

PNG's improvement over the past decade has been steady, but it is about to hit overdrive. This game against England might be the last dance for the Kumuls as we've come to know them.

2. The New Zealand duo closing in on history

Casey McLean seemingly cannot stop scoring tries for New Zealand. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde )

It was another Kiwi romp as New Zealand punished a Fiji side that struggled to backup from last week's fine performance against Australia, but amid the near-endless tries and ill-tempered flare-ups, Casey McLean and Jamayne Isaako continued their march towards history.

Isaako scored 26 points from a try and 13 goals from as many attempts to go with his 38 points against the Cook Islands the weeks before, and the winger is closing in on Shaun Johnson's all-time Kiwi pointscoring record.

The former Dolphin has 215 points from his 17 Tests, just 10 shy of Johnson's mark, and could claim top spot as early as the World Cup final if the points continue to flow for Stacey Jones's side.

McLean has more work to do to run down Manu Vatuvei as the nation's highest-ever try-scorer, but he is making a cracking pace.

In just seven Tests, McLean has scored 15 tries to sit in equal-eighth spot on the all-time list. Every other player around him had at least 20 caps, and Vatuvei took 29 to collect his 23 tries.

The second four-try haul of his budding career means that at just 20, McLean is odds on to become New Zealand's Test try-scoring king sooner rather than later.

3. Are Australia still the favourites?

Australia has done enough to qualify for the semifinals. (Getty Images: Ian Hitchcock)

The Kangaroos are one of only two unbeaten sides heading into the knockout phase, but their hold on favouritism is shaky at best.

Their brilliant win over New Zealand in the tournament opener had more than a few elements of fortune in their favour, especially the two length-of-the-field intercept tries that kept them in the game early on.

They scratched their way past Fiji and romped home against the Cook Islands since, looking short of their best in both performances.

While they are always a threat, it feels as though all four nations in the semifinals are in with a chance of lifting the trophy rather than it being Australia's birthright.

Kevin Walters has a big decision to make at halfback between Tom Dearden and Sam Walker but seems to have settled on Reece Walsh as his custodian, and after the Broncos playmaker laid on five tries in this 66-6 mauling to go with his game-changing plays against the Kiwis, it's hard to argue.

4. Lebanon-France is what the World Cup can be

Abbas Miski's miracle try was one of the moments of the World Cup. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

After a tournament filled with blowouts, the epic finish between France and Lebanon shows what's possible when things line up right at the World Cup, as two winless teams desperate to restore some pride played out a classic.

This was two teams of similar skill levels in front of a rowdy and emotionally invested crowd at a venue that accentuated at least one of the fan bases.

That's a simple recipe to follow, and while you won't always be rewarded with the epic finish of this golden point thriller, a new format that keeps teams like this together and therefore produces more of these match-ups is a must for 2030.

When that next tournament rolls around, plenty of tales from this game will be told, from Cesar Rouge's game-winning field goal controversially chalked off the board to Lebanon's remarkable extra-time try to Abbas Miski.

That score put the tragedy of French fullback Arthur Mourgue, a mad genius who doesn't always nail the genius part, into World Cup folklore after his remarkable field goal sent the game to extra time before a maniac kick inside his own 20 fell for the Cedars's winning try.

5. The veteran Tonga cannot do without

Tui Lolohea had another role to play in another epic win for Tonga. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

Amid a match with a galaxy of stars that promised a glorious future for Samoa and Tonga, Tui Lolohea seemed the odd man out.

The Tongan veteran was the only player in the game who doesn't ply his trade in the NRL, and given his mercurial career, he might have seemed a weak link for the Mate Ma'a.

But after 12 seasons in the red jersey, Lolohea has proven himself an invaluable part of their rise to the top of Test football, and while they have more talent at their disposal than ever before, they always come back to him when it counts.

Along with Jason Taumalolo, Lolohea is the only man to have played in each of Tonga's most important wins over the past decade and always seems to defy critics when it matters most.

He is older and slower, but he always gives Tonga what they need — the 31-year-old, who currently doesn't have a club for next season, set up a try for Jojo Fifita with a clever floating pass and held up well in defence under heavy pressure from Samoa, who clearly targeted the former Huddersfield Giant.

With Latu Fainu fit and Talatau Amone in the squad, Tonga are not short of options in the halves, but Lolohea rewarded coach Kristian Woolf's faith yet again, as he always seems to do when it matters most.

title: Labor allegedly used threats and inflated costs to dictate Airport Rail Link
text:
The Victorian opposition has accused Labor of "bullying and intimidation" after reported allegations that project costs were deliberately inflated and a senior public servant was threatened into supporting the government's preferred plans for the Melbourne Airport Rail Link.

An anonymous submission by a former government planning expert to Victoria's royal commission into the construction industry, first reported by The Age, reportedly said the government had chosen a route for the rail link through the suburb of Sunshine as its preferred project and intentionally undermined other routes with increased cost estimates.

To do so, the planning expert said between $3.8 billion and $4.6 billion of unnecessary tunnelling was added to an alternate Maribyrnong route to make it a less attractive option.

Shadow Minister for Transport Infrastructure Evan Mulholland blasted the government over the allegations.

Evan Mulholland says Ben Carroll must tell Victorians what he knew of the allegations around the Airport Rail Link. (ABC News: Simon Winter)

"We've seen revelations that Jacinta Allan and her office allegedly bullied, threatened and intimidated senior public servants to get a preferred political outcome on the Melbourne Airport Rail," he said.

He said Premier Ben Carroll would have been in cabinet at the time of the allegations, and pushed the premier to reveal his own knowledge of events.

"He needs to explain what he knew, and when he knew it," Mr Mulholland said.

The proposed Sunshine route will see a new station built at Keilor East connecting it with the airport and metro network, and falls within Mr Carroll's electorate of Niddrie.

Multiple routes were proposed for the Melbourne Airport rail link in 2018 after then-Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull pledged up to $5 billion to build the link. (ABC News )

In response to the allegations, the state government said it would not pre-empt the findings of the royal commission by commenting.

"The premier's first act was to establish the toughest royal commission into the construction industry to leave no stone unturned," a spokesperson said.

"The terms of reference are broad and expansive. Nothing is off limits."

Senior government minister Jaclyn Symes threw cold water over the allegations, casting doubt on their veracity.

"In terms of reading some of the allegations in the paper, there isn't even sources in relation to some of these claims," she said.

The expert told The Age that when he raised the issue with executives he was threatened with losing his job if he did not confirm Sunshine as the ideal route for the project.

The sacking threat allegedly came from the minister for public transport and major projects at the time, Jacinta Allan.

A spokesperson for Ms Allan denied the allegations and said the former premier would cooperate fully with the royal commission.

Jacinta Allan was the minister for public transport infrastructure and major projects at the time of the alleged events. (ABC News)

Mr Mulholland said the Coalition would not divert from the plans to build the route through Sunshine if elected, as work had already begun.

"Contracted works are already underway, the route is the route, we will get on and do it," he said.

Integrity expert says fresh allegations could be just the beginning

Centre for Public Integrity researcher William Partlett said today's allegations were concerning, and reflected a "culture of impunity" when it came to the government's handling of major infrastructure projects.

"This is just the issue of what's happening inside the black box of the executive," he said.

"If these allegations are true, there seemed to be an assumption in the government and the minister that this was largely something that they could do, they'd do without any oversight."

Construction of an airport rail link in Melbourne has been a political talking point for decades, with successive governments each proposing their own vision. (Supplied: Victorian government)

Dr Partlett said the allegations of intimidation were also concerning and reflected the weakness and under-resourcing of the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission (IBAC) at the time.

The anonymous source said they kept silent on the incident due to fears of having their career derailed, and later quit the department.

"There was a view that it was too risky to go to IBAC when there were significant concerns about what that would mean for the careers for these individuals, whistleblowers in the future," Professor Partlett said.

In September, the state government passed legislation to strengthen the powers of IBAC, as part of a campaign to restore trust in government.

But Dr Partlett said the government's pledge for transparency and accountability could see even more allegations come to light.

"The momentum has shifted ... I wouldn't be surprised if we're going to see even more allegations in the coming weeks and months," he said.

The ABC approached the Royal Commission into the Integrity of Major Public and Civil Infrastructure Construction Projects in Victoria for comment.

title: Large crocodile spotted near future Olympic rowing course
text:
The sighting of a saltwater crocodile near the proposed 2032 Olympic rowing precinct in Rockhampton is under investigation, while Rowing Australia says it is a "shock" and a wake-up call.

North Rockhampton Golf Club alerted members at the weekend when the crocodile, estimated to be up to 3 metres long, was spotted near the 11th hole.

The sighting was within a few kilometres of the Fitzroy River precinct earmarked for rowing and canoe sprint events at the 2032 Brisbane Olympic and Paralympic Games.

The selection of Rockhampton as the home of the Games' rowing has been questioned by some. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

On Monday, a spokesperson for the Department of the Environment, Tourism, Science and Innovation (DETSI) said the sighting was not reported to the department, but was now under investigation.

Speaking in Hervey Bay on Monday morning, Queensland Premier David Crisafulli played down concerns about the crocodile and expressed confidence in Rockhampton's ability to host the Olympic rowing events.

"Many, many decades of success prove that it's a world-class venue," he said.

"It's a magnificent community and they'll do it very, very well."

David Crisafulli has backed Rockhampton's rowing venue amid renewed crocodile concerns. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

Rowing Australia life member Ray Ebert said the sighting was a wake-up call for those involved in planning the 2032 Olympic rowing events on the Fitzroy River.

"It's a bit of a shock to me," Mr Ebert told ABC News Breakfast on Monday.

"I've been saying that the crocodiles are the least of our problems. I'm going to admit to something that none of the politicians have admitted to: maybe I was wrong."

Mr Ebert pointed to previous crocodile sightings in the area, including two reported in December 2024, involving animals measuring about 2.5 metres and 1 metre.

Loading...

He said the latest sighting raised questions about how authorities would manage crocodile risks around the proposed rowing venue.

"It's not the crocodiles that you can see that I would be worried about. It's the ones that I can't see," he said.

Mr Ebert questioned whether the Queensland government was taking the issue seriously enough and said the sighting could prompt further questions about the venue's suitability and safety.

Rowing venue scrutiny

State and national rowing regattas have been held on the Fitzroy River and the venue has also been used by Australian rowing teams for pre-Olympic training camps over the years.

In September, Mr Crisafulli announced the Rockhampton venue had passed an independent technical assessment "with flying colours" to host rowing and canoe sprint events at the 2032 Brisbane Games.

It came after months of fierce debate over the Fitzroy River's suitability, including its status as a crocodile habitat.

The Rockhampton rowing facility has hosted multiple events. (Supplied: Rockhampton Fitzroy Rowing Club)

International sporting bodies are now awaiting the next phase of venue planning, which include technical details and confirmation of service levels and facilities needed for Olympic and Paralympic competitions.

Queensland Opposition Leader Steven Miles said the sighting highlighted the need for the Crisafulli government to release the technical report underpinning Rockhampton's selection as an Olympic rowing venue.

Mr Miles said the report should outline how crocodile risks would be managed during the Games, arguing its release would help address concerns about the Fitzroy River.

A sign at the North Rockhampton Golf Club warns visitors of crocodiles on the course. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

University of Queensland crocodile expert and emeritus professor Craig Franklin was more critical of the decision to hold Olympic rowing on the Fitzroy River.

He described it as a political decision rather than one based on common sense, saying he would go so far as to call it "foolish".

On September 19, a saltwater croc was spotted upstream from the Rockhampton rowing course, according to the Queensland government's official sightings dashboard.

There have been two further sightings since that were reported closer to the proposed venue.

Croc expert supports removal

Reptile expert John Lever, who owns Koorana Crocodile Farm near Rockhampton, said the animal was likely to be a male saltwater crocodile and estimated it was "up to three metres" long based on the photograph of the sighting.

Mr Lever said wildlife rangers would likely need to assess the animal's behaviour before a decision was made about whether it should be removed.

Koorana Crocodile Farm owner John Lever. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

The area is not currently classified as a Category A zone, where crocodiles are automatically targeted for removal.

However, Mr Lever said he believed crocodiles spotted in the vicinity of the planned Olympic venue should be dealt with.

"With the Olympics coming up, my take on this would be that any crocodile seen in that area should be removed," he said.

"But that's not up to me to do that, it's up to the government."

A DETSI spokesperson said the Queensland Crocodile Management Plan was reviewed every year.

The Fitzroy River has faced intense scrutiny since its selection as an Olympic venue. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

Mr Lever said heavy rainfall in central Queensland last week may have stimulated the animal's activity.

"There's crocodiles, of course, in the Fitzroy [River], we all know that, so a sighting is not uncommon," he said.

"This is the mating season. Males and females are both moving around looking for mates."

title: Tasmania might keep public transport free statewide
text:
The Tasmanian government says it is considering keeping public transport across the state free indefinitely.

In March, the state government announced public transport would be free for three months in response to high fuel prices.

It later extended that until July 2027 in the state budget, at a cost of $24 million.

Transport Minister Kerry Vincent has now confirmed the government is in the process of working out whether it can afford to keep public transport free indefinitely.

"The numbers have been fantastic with the growth in various areas," he said.

"What we'd need to do is just weigh up the cost of that, how we operate Metro and our general access buses all around the state.

"And understand the impact that has of moving more people off our roads and onto public transport."

New ticketing system project on pause

The state government has a contract with Cubic to develop a new electronic ticketing system for public transport.

Building Tasmania said the contract was worth $27.7 million, with $11.9 million already paid to date.

Last year's annual report said the common ticketing system would end up costing $65 million, but the government later said that figure was incorrect and down to human error.

The government is considering whether or not to keep public transport free. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Mr Vincent today said the ticketing system was on pause while the government considered all its options.

He was unable to say whether there were consequences for pulling out of the contract.

"We have a contract in place, and we've been working through various bits of information that they have available as part of the package to us, and I haven't all those details at that time," he said.

The minister said there were no targets in place when working out whether free public transport would pay off, but he did want to see an increase in numbers.

"Tasmania's never really taken public transport on board like most major metropolitan areas," he said.

"So we need to keep increasing the numbers and see the benefits that are flowing to the community and measure that against what we're up against with building more roads, replacing roads.

" So it's a balancing act but we're working through that on a monthly basis. "

Even if public transport remains free, the government might look at having a passenger counting system to help it understand demand.

Likely to incentivise more trips, expert says

Transport consultant Steven Burgess said keeping public transport free makes it more convenient and more accessible for people.

But he said a lot of the increase in trips was down to people taking extra trips rather than people moving from cars to public transport.

"A lot of it is trips that couldn't be made before or … instead of going to the city once this week, I can go twice," he said.

"Now it's free, we're getting new trips, which can be great. People [are] coming to the city more often, they can do more stuff, create more opportunities.

" Not all of it is saving us traffic, [it's] not necessarily a congestion buster, but it does get people around a bit easier. "

But Mr Burgess said the government would also need to look at the equity of the current service.

"Making it free across the board is a bit inequitable because the suburbs that have the best bus service … are the wealthy suburbs," he said.

"There are some suburbs, our out-of-fringe suburbs, where it's a different financial demographic out there, and those people have very low-quality services and they need investment.

"If it's going to be permanent, there's going to need to be some massive investment in PT to provide some equity to the service so everyone gets a go at this really, really expensive service the government is investing in."

title: Bancroft reaches acceptance over Test recall chances after 'dejection'
text:
Cameron Bancroft says his passion to return to the Australian Test side has faded as the national team scrambles for a solution to its batting woes following a disastrous Cape Town collapse.

Australia returned to Cape Town last week for the first time since the infamous 2018 sandpaper scandal that saw Bancroft banished from Test selection.

As the national side capitulated in the series decider, Bancroft recorded his 34th first class century and 15th in seven years, hammering 186 for Western Australia against South Australia in the Sheffield Shield at Adelaide Oval.

Strategy, succession planning needed for Australia after Cape Town collapse After a disastrous series loss to South Africa, Australian cricket faces some tough decisions, writes Russell Jackson.

"I'm definitely not as feverish now about my opportunities to play at that level," Bancroft told ABC Sport's Summer Grandstand.

"I'm fully accepting of the fact that the likelihood is that I won't play at that level again. If an opportunity came I'd be very grateful and I'd take it, but I'm at peace with playing at the level and the opportunity I had there."

Despite being the leading run-scorer in the 2022/23 Shield season and second in the 2023/24 campaign for WA, Bancroft wasn't selected for the Test series against the West Indies and Pakistan that summer, with selectors opting for David Warner to complete a retirement tour and then trialling Steve Smith in the opener position.

Bancroft revealed he still isn't quite sure why he wasn't picked despite his strong domestic form.

"It's a great question. I'm not sure … it just didn't go my way," he said.

Cameron Bancroft has remained a prolific run scorer at the Sheffield Shield level but remains out of favour with the Australian selectors. (Getty Images: Mark Brake)

"Naturally you feel a bit of dejection. It did bring me down for sure. When you want something so badly and you feel like you've given 100 per cent and it's not quite enough; naturally you feel those emotions.

"The reasons why you play and enjoy the game get questioned. A big part of my own career is finding peace with that."

The Australian men's side has now had nine different opening combinations in their past 19 Tests and is facing a race against time to find a solution, with a home series against New Zealand in December and overseas tours of India and England in 2027.

Bancroft believes the national team is lacking chemistry due to the inconsistent nature of the top order.

"There's no doubt continuity is something that has been lacking a little bit," he said.

"From the outside there's lots of changes and thoughts and theories. It's probably something that hasn't been figured out or solved yet."

title: Strintzos eyes Olympic berth after fifth finish in New York Marathon
text:
Australia's Haftu Strintzos has taken a giant step towards the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles by finishing fifth at the New York City Marathon, the year's final and arguably toughest major.

Strintzos crossed the line in 2:06:34, only 33 seconds behind Sweden's Andreas Almgren, who won on his marathon debut in 2:06:01. He was also just 14 seconds off his Australian record of 2:06:20, set at the Gold Coast Marathon in July.

"I am happy with the performance today as it is my second race ever at a world major," said Strintzos.

"My focus is always on performance, and I gave myself a shot to get on the podium."

Loading...

"Close, but not quite there yet."

Under World Athletics' LA28 qualification system, a top-five finish at a Platinum Label marathon during the qualifying window counts as meeting the Olympic entry standard.

The window opened on 1 November, so Strintzos's result counts, although Olympic places remain subject to selection by Australian Athletics, which will happen in 2028.

"I fought all the way to the finish line to secure a fifth-place finish and it's exciting to get the auto qualifier for the Olympics," he said.

The 27-year-old was one of six men to break 2:07 in New York overnight, compared with seven in the previous 54 editions of the race combined.

Splits shared by his Adelaide-based coach Adam Didyk show Strintzos ran a patient, controlled race with a strong negative split. He went through halfway in 64:06 and ran the second half 1:38 faster, in 62:28.

His opening 5km was his slowest of the race, at 15:34, or about 3:07 per kilometre. He settled to roughly 3:00 per km between the 10 and 20km markers, before lifting the pace through the middle stages. His last 2.2km was his quickest of the race, at 2:52 per km.

That closing speed is what Didyk has said Strintzos will need to be competitive at world championship or Olympic level.

"The long-term goal is to develop Haftu into a championship performer, an athlete who gets it right when it counts," said Didyk.

"Championship marathons are won by racing smart, being patient and having something left over the last 10 kilometres. Today was a big step in that direction."

The result came on the challenging point-to-point route from Staten Island to Central Park, famous for its bridges, crowds and tactical racing rather than fast times. Athletes commonly put New York a few minutes slower than flatter courses such as Valencia, Berlin or Chicago.

"Our plan coming into New York was clear: race for a top-five finish. We weren't chasing a time," said Didyk.

"Today was a good example of what that racing looks like."

Kenya's Sheila Chepkirui claimed her second women's title in three years, running 2:24:36 to edge clear of defending champion Hellen Obiri late in the race.

title: He used to ride bulls. Now he takes calls from the King and has seven Cup runners
text:

Don’t let leading horse trainer Ciaron Maher’s laid-back demeanour be your lasting impression. His mind is like a steel trap. Asked whether he recalled a horse called Electric Turban, he did not miss a beat. “Yeah, that was one of Richard Freyer’s,” Maher said. It is also the most recent horse he rode around the two miles at Flemington, where he will race seven horses on Tuesday in the Melbourne Cup. Loading That ride happened way back in April 2002 when Maher was a tearaway jumps jockey who had moved from Warrnambool to live at the end of the Flemington straight with a bunch of other aspiring jockeys. Maher finished fourth on Electric Turban midway through his career in the saddle that was never going to go far given his size. He rode a respectable 26 winners from 210 rides and finished third in the Brierly Steeplechase at Warrnambool on Yallah Limit in 2002.

Advertisement

“Safe to say that I was better on the other side of the fence,” Maher said. But he recalls with fondness the vibe among jumps jockeys on Melbourne Cup Day as the lesser lights raced in the Cup Hurdle, which was won and done before midday, allowing them to settle in for a big day with family and friends. His only ride in the Cup Hurdle came 26 years ago on Taylors Bridge for the late Peter Hayes. Maher’s mount sat back in the field and just managed to avoid a fallen horse, Gilligan, and finished seventh. Later that day Brew won the big one from the outside barrier. Was he a mad bugger in those days? It’s a reputation the rest of the jumps jockey fraternity used to wear as a badge of honour. ”Some would say I still am,” he said with a wry grin. Despite the pressure of expectation a smile never seems far from Ciaron Maher’s face. Getty Images He hides the madness well, running the country’s biggest training operation with a calmness that seems to translate to his horses. His business has about 900 horses and operates out of six locations – three in Victoria and three in NSW.

Advertisement

The systems and planning required is astounding. Maher invests heavily in science, data analysis and horse wellbeing. What puts Maher among the elite trainers, however, is not the whizz bang devices or the high-performance staff. It’s his desire to learn about horses, which has not diminished from the moment his mum, Eileen, dropped him off at trainer Shayne Fisher’s property near the family dairy farm in Winslow, in Victoria’s south-west, when he was just out of primary school. Fisher, a hugely respected horseman around Warrnambool, laughs at the memories of a bunch of local kids including Ciaron and his brother Declan, his own stepson, Australian equestrian champion Jamie Kermond, and others hanging out at his property on weeknights. On weekends, they would jump in his truck to attend showjumping, pony club events or shetland steeplechase races. “He spent a lot of time at our place,” Fisher recalled. “He was very keen and wanted to have a go at everything. They were wild buggers, got into bull riding and all sorts of things. They weren’t just little kids sitting on the sidelines.

Advertisement

Ciaron Maher and then co-trainer David Eustace won the Melbourne Cup in 2022 with Gold Trip. Jason South “They got to learn the basics with every horse, not just horseracing. We taught them the basics of horse handling,” Fisher said. They became tough, too. Fisher laughed as he recalled Maher one day squealing that he could not stop a horse he was riding only to be told, “point him at the shed”. That, apparently, would encourage the horse to pull up. Maher became an apprentice, before moving to the city to work with the Hayes stable. However, once he turned his attention to training in late 2005, Fisher realised the youngster’s aspirations in that field exceeded his own. Maher didn’t just want to be a trainer, he wanted to be Victoria’s leading trainer. Maher hadn’t wasted his time as a jumps jockey. That speciality requires riders to work with the animal rather than just jumping on their back, often breaking or pre-training horses or doing trackwork. Former jumps jockeys trained the winners of both the Caulfield Cup and Cox Plate this year.

Advertisement

“Normally the jumps jocks are riding the difficult horses,” Maher said. “That [time] was phenomenal for me.” As a track rider he worked for greats such as Bart Cummings, Jim Houlahan and Paddy Payne. He then rode in Ireland and, later, worked there as well, storing the lessons every moment provided. “I never took notes, but I do think about every little thing [I experienced] when a scenario comes up [now],” Maher said. Maher’s first breakthrough as a trainer came when, on the final day of the 2007 Flemington carnival, the gelding Tears I Cry won the group 1 mile at huge odds. He had only been a trainer for two years and after spending time preparing horses out of his parents’ dairy farm in Warrnambool, he moved into two boxes at Caulfield alongside racing greats such as Peter Moody, Mick Price and Rick Hore-Lacey. He had been told if he stayed near home, all he could hope to train were broken-down types from owners hoping for a miracle. His mum thought he would be back in Warrnambool in no time, but he settled in with the experienced crew working their horses there and expanded his operation, winning the 2016 Caulfield Cup with Jameka.

When he was serving jail time in 2024, the crypto exchange billionaire Changpeng Zhao wrote a book with a modest title: Freedom of Money: A Memoir of Protecting Users, Resilience, and the Founding of Binance. The tome was short on introspection. A $US50 million ($71.2 million) personal fine, $US4.3 billion company penalty and four-month stretch in prison for failing to run an effective anti-money laundering scheme were like water off a duck’s back. Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao needs other cryptocurrency exchanges to block suspicious transactions. Bloomberg In one irony-free observation, Zhao wrote of being in jail that “the entire process was designed to deliver the lowest possible customer satisfaction.” The book did little too to explain how Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, has protected its users, except where that is a byproduct of its own rapid growth. Since last Friday, when hackers stole $US6.3 billion in tokens from his website, Zhao has had a chance to turn his words into reality.

Advertisement

If Binance’s announcements since the hack are to be believed, the former chief executive has done a good job of compensating, if not protecting, his users. After a feverish weekend of work, Binance announced on Monday that it had covered 95 per cent of the stolen tokens by value through its unfortunately named SAFU – Security Asset Fund for Users – program and resumed withdrawals. Related Article Cryptocurrencies Inside the scramble to contain the largest crypto heist in history That may turn out to be the easy part. If Binance is to actually get back the billions in tokens that were stolen, Zhao will have to hope that other cryptocurrency companies have better anti-money laundering processes than his firm once did. According to the FBI, the heist was likely carried out by a North Korean hacking group known as TraderTraitor. Early indications suggest that once the hackers started moving tokens, the entire $US6.3 billion was pulled out within half an hour. At that point, much of the haul was in stablecoins such as Tether and Circle, which are designed to track the price of another asset, such as the US dollar. But the hackers rapidly started exchanging those tokens for truly decentralised alternatives, such as Bitcoin and Ethereum. The difference is that Tether and Circle can be frozen by the tech companies that created them; Bitcoin and Ethereum are the wild west.

Advertisement

The cryptocurrency tracking company Chainalysis noted that about half of the stolen coins were frozen by law enforcement and industry players before that could happen. That has put all eyes on the remaining $US3.3 billion worth of coins, which are now pinging between different cryptocurrency platforms, wallets and coins as the hackers try to avoid the watching eyes of law enforcement and crypto analysis companies. Their likely end goal? Convert the money into traditional currency, such as US dollars or Chinese yuan, that the North Korean regime can actually use. Cryptocurrency thefts are perfect for that purpose. Where a traditional hack – and North Korea has executed several, including the Wannacry breach that hit the UK’s National Health Service or the 2014 Sony Pictures attack – might result in the release of sensitive data, mass disruption or a ransom payment in the millions, targeting a big crypto exchange can net billions. In his book, Zhao frames his jail time as a disproportionate punishment for a minor record keeping issue. The US government disagreed, arguing in court that Binance had failed to stop hundreds of millions of dollars in unlawful transactions, including for sanctioned Iranian entities and drug traffickers. Zhao has since been pardoned by US President Donald Trump. He may have moved on, but to stop Binance users’ stolen funds being swapped for traditional money, Zhao needs other cryptocurrency exchanges to do much better at detecting malicious users than Binance did – at least in the past. title: I’ve been to an Ivy League college – our universities are failing at one vital job
text:

NationalUniversity Opinion I’ve been to an Ivy League college – our universities are failing at one vital job Allegra Schubert University student November 2, 2026 — 3:35pm

November 2, 2026 — 3:35pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I returned from my exchange at the University of Pennsylvania with no fewer than 10 T-shirts and jumpers, an assortment of posters and pins, a mug, several tote bags and, much to my surprise, Penn-branded socks. I went to Philadelphia halfway through a five-and-a-half-year degree at the University of Sydney, wanting more than a reprieve from the routine. I returned with something less portable than merchandise: a nagging suspicion that Australian universities are failing to prepare us for life after graduation. Allegra Schubert (pictured right) studies at Sydney University but went to the University of Pennsylvania on exchange. Let me dispel one myth early. The content was not harder. My subjects were pitched at roughly the same level as their USyd equivalents and assessed in much the same way, with a similar weekly workload. If you were hoping for a tale of Ivy League rigour flattening a hapless Australian, I can’t oblige. What differed was the delivery. My professors wrote everything by hand on a blackboard, working through each problem in real time. At home, lecturers often display pre-typed solutions and narrate over them, which is efficient but, I find, ultimately detrimental to the learning experience. Penn’s lectures weren’t compulsory, but they weren’t recorded either. Miss one and your sole recourse was a friend’s notes, so attendance became self-enforcing. Small weekly homework tasks, worth only a few per cent of the grade, obliged me to consolidate each week’s material instead of exhuming it in the final fortnight.

Advertisement

Then there was the cold calling. In classes small enough to allow it, everyone was called on once or twice a session. At USyd, a participation mark can usually be secured with one perfunctory comment, after which you are free to drift off. For someone who had never voluntarily raised a hand in an Australian lecture, this was petrifying. It was also where I learnt the most because I spent every minute knowing I might be next on the chopping block. Related Article Editorial

University Falling university rankings suggest a wider malaise The Herald's View Editorial By the end of semester, my professors knew almost every student by name. At USyd, that relationship is largely outsourced to tutors, usually postgraduate students and, in my early years, undergraduates barely older than me. The biggest difference of all were the students. Every American I met could articulate precisely why they were doing their degree and where it would take them. Second-year students outlined career trajectories that ran, without apparent irony, all the way to retirement. They also asked questions. Constantly. They volunteered answers with no fear of being wrong and posed silly questions without a flicker of embarrassment. Australian lecture theatres, in my experience, are very different. They typically play out as follows: the lecturer pleads for a response, endures a long silence, then supplies the answer themselves. Tall poppy syndrome, as far as I could tell, had not been granted a visa.

Advertisement

This was the part that unsettled me. Three years into a dual degree, I was not sure where it was leading, and neither are most of my Australian university friends. I don’t think my American classmates are any more intelligent than us. They had simply been asked, much earlier and much more insistently, what they wanted to do with their lives. Related Article Education ‘Wake-up call’ as Australian universities slip in world rankings For high-demand courses, an Australian teenager’s future hinges on a few weeks of exams in Year 12, distilled into a single number. American students carry that pressure across years of grades, testing, sport and side projects, and are nudged from the start of high school to work out what genuinely interests them. I am a case study in what happens without that nudge. My ATAR, not my ambition, chose my degree. Like many of my friends, I was backed into a corner by a number. The American approach, to be clear, is no utopia. It favours families who can pay for private tutoring and admissions consultants. Still, it makes teenagers confront a question that we put off for half a decade.

Advertisement

Another difference is how American universities compete for enrolments. The top universities chase the same students by focusing on the experience. Some campuses have gone as far as building lazy rivers; at Penn, faculties hosted dinners, the Dean threw a formal, and societies handed out doughnuts and sodas by the armful. My sock drawer, I now realise, was a line item in a marketing budget. Related Article Opinion

High school If your child starts year 12 exams today, don’t do what I did Margot Saville Deputy opinion editor Australia’s roughly 40 universities are almost all public, large and broadly comparable, and with domestic fees regulated, their fiercest contest is for international students. The domestic student experience is largely overlooked. The 2025 Student Experience Survey found that only 37.3 per cent of domestic undergraduates enrolled on campus attended all their classes in person. Of those, 54.4 per cent felt a sense of belonging, compared with 45.5 per cent of students who mixed online and in-person classes. I’m not suggesting Australia import the American system, price tag and inequity included. But much of what made Penn’s classrooms work would cost very little here. Lecturers could work through problems by hand and cold call in classes small enough to allow it. The people who set the exam could learn the names of the people sitting it. If high school is too late to fix, universities must pick up the slack. In Australia, the name on your testamur rarely sets you apart. What distinguishes a graduate is what they did beyond the syllabus: the project they built, the team they played in, the society they ran. Universities should push students towards these from first year. Most of us, after all, are here to land a career and an income that can support the life we want to live.

Advertisement

Penn won me over with socks. Australian universities, I’m asking you for something worth far more: graduates who walk out knowing what they want to do next and how to achieve it. Allegra Schubert is studying Commerce/Engineering at the University of Sydney.
