title: Cape Town was the batting collapse we had to have. Now selectors must make changes
text:
Advertisement

SportCricketTest cricket Opinion Cape Town was the batting collapse we had to have. Now selectors must make changes Greg Chappell Former Australian Test captain November 2, 2026 — 3:30pm

November 2, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Paul Keating called the early-1990s economic downturn “the recession we had to have.” Similarly, Australia’s 111 in the fourth innings at Newlands was the collapse we had to have. Whether anyone learns from it is another matter. I disagree with Pat Cummins that this is a very good side. It has been an excellent bowling side for a long time, but even the bowlers failed to trouble South Africa at crucial times. The Proteas batters had a plan in the second innings to let the short balls go and make the Australians bowl to them. Simon Harmer bowled South Africa to victory over Australia in Cape Town. AP Photo/Halden Krog It was hard to discern any plan from our batters in their second innings in Cape Town. The Australian batting hasn’t carried its weight for some time, and a team holding a substantial first-innings lead doesn’t fold for 111 in the second innings if the batting is sound. The scoreboard doesn’t lie. I take no pleasure in saying so. I’ve been a batsman, captain, selector and coach, and I’d rather be building than knocking.

Advertisement

I sat in a few dressing rooms after humbling experiences, but with straight shooters like Ian Chappell, Keith Stackpole and Rod Marsh, we were never allowed to pretend that we were just unlucky. It was shape up, or ship out. Pat sees talent and good intent in that room, and he’s right. But to some extent a team operates in a bubble, and inside it every failure is bad luck. From outside, it looks different. Loading Start with the toss. Plenty thought bowling first on a good Cape Town pitch was a mistake, and I suspect Kagiso Rabada running through our top order was the biggest factor. Then we batted last on a surface that has historically helped spin late. A self-inflicted double whammy. We beat South Africa without Rabada in Durban, and that flattered us. But the toss is the least of it.

Advertisement

For years the selectors have patched the batting with experienced first-class players who look reliable on paper. The result is a middle order heavy with age and short on resilience. The names of Michael Hussey and Adam Gilchrist are often trotted out in defence of this approach. Hussey made mountains of runs for Western Australia and would have played much earlier if he hadn’t been stuck behind one of the best line-ups ever. Gilchrist went across the Nullarbor because NSW wouldn’t give him a regular game. Both were blocked, and both were once-in-a-generation players. You can’t build a selection policy on them. Pat Cummins bats on day five. AP Photo/Halden Krog The states aren’t blameless. Sheffield Shield sides pick safe experience over potential, so the national panel is choosing from a pool shaped by caution. Matt Renshaw’s 369 runs at 61.5 was the best news of the tour, and he muddies my argument. He first played for Australia at the age of 20, making 184 against Pakistan at the SCG, then got dropped three times. It was nine years before he made his second hundred. Patience works, say the defenders of the status quo.

Advertisement

I don’t buy it. Renshaw was never a journeyman. We threw away a talent and then had to look for it again. In Durban, we were 4-84 when he came in, and he made 190 off 397 balls. He faced 115 balls on the first day for three boundaries, reached 50 off the second ball of the second morning and put on 134 for the ninth wicket with Nathan Lyon. Matt Renshaw should open the batting for Australia. Getty Images He left well and hit anything straight. A bouncer found his grille, and he just carried on. His words afterwards told you what the chance meant to him. I lost my place in the Test team early in my career and wondered if I really belonged. It was only for a few weeks, so I can’t imagine what it must feel like to be on the outside for most of a decade. Renshaw is 30 now, and he’s back because the selectors ran out of options, not because anyone had a plan. Imagine what we’d have if we’d kept faith with him in 2017 and let him grow inside the side. That’s the lesson of his story.

Advertisement

It also settles the question that’s bugged the selectors since David Warner retired. Renshaw leaves the ball well, is hard to shift, and he sees off the new ball. He batted at five in Durban, but his game is built for the top of the order. Renshaw opens. Selector must put Marnus Labuschagne out of his misery. Getty Images The identity of his partner is the next problem. Travis Head thrives at home, where pace and bounce suit him down to the ground. On lower, slower pitches overseas, his slashing game gets exposed. He is caught in the infield or drags on to his stumps. I’m not convinced he’s an opener away from Australia. Cameron Green looks better since his injury, but his early footwork worries me. He’s so intent on survival that he takes short strides to full balls, which leaves his contact point well in front of his eyes. The hands get pushed out, the face opens, and there’s a gap between bat and pad. Against spin, it’s worse: short strides leave you short of the pitch of the ball, and the hands have too much to do. He needs a longer first stride, with the contact point under his eyes. Running down the pitch to defend against a spinner is a sure way to promote short strides.

Advertisement

I experienced similar problems at various times in my career and made a conscious effort to exaggerate my footwork in net sessions to train a longer forward stride. Cam has enormous levers, but he is not using them. He must smother the seam movement and spin, or he won’t be the player he could be. Josh Inglis wants to score, not survive. Green ran him out in the second innings, but Inglis has done enough for at least another series. Then there is Marnus Labuschagne. The selectors cannot dodge it any longer. I call it elite performance decline: the older player starts to doubt himself. Steve Waugh admitted that late in his career the mental effort outweighed the joy. I think Marnus is there. The kindest thing the selectors can do is put him out of his misery. Drop him for the summer and send him back to domestic cricket. Ban the video analysis too. He’s spent years studying himself when he should be watching the ball. Strip away the triggers, guard changes and endless tinkering, and let him go back to hitting it. Looking ahead, I’d make Cricket Australia do something about the states. Tie funding and academy resources to debuting and developing young players in the top four. Then look at Oliver Davies, who wants to score and puts the bowler under pressure. Look at Sam Konstas, with his classical high-elbow technique. Look at Campbell Kellaway, who has the desire to occupy the crease all day.

Advertisement

Related Article Australian cricket Coach calls for calm, keeps door ajar for Labuschagne, as Healy turns torch on selectors The selectors will be back at the drawing board for New Zealand, but those conditions will be familiar and suit our pace attack, which covers a lot of cracks. India is a different story. Turning pitches blunt the quicks and expose a fragile batting line-up. The road back to the Test final is full of potholes. Newlands wasn’t only about talent. It was about a system afraid of risk, one that papers over cracks with domestic veterans while first-class cricket decays into a white-ball shadow. If Cricket Australia and the states hide behind platitudes, the home summer will be harder than it needs to be. If they take the shock, this can be the correction that sets us right. title: Dees sweat on injury ahead of blockbuster AFLW final; Freo turn to Wharfie Time … but fail to score

Sydney have confirmed their home AFLW elimination final against the Western Bulldogs after overcoming Wharfie Time and a horror injury to beat Fremantle by one point.

Play was held up for 10 minutes in the first quarter on Sunday at Cockburn before Swans ruck Caitlin Reid was stretchered from the field. She was felled by a clash of heads with Fremantle’s Hayley Miller.

After Sydney rallied in the second half and took the lead, Miller snapped a goal to bring the Dockers to within one point and Wharfie Time was sounded, with less than 90 seconds on the clock.

But just as the crowd activation backfired horribly in the AFL grand final loss to Brisbane, the Dockers could not score again.

Chloe Molloy took a game-saving mark with 15 seconds left and the Swans won 5.7 (37) to 5.6 (36), denying Dockers star Ash Brazill a farewell win.

Molloy kicked four goals to break the AFLW goalkicking record with 28, two up on Hawthorn’s Aine McDonagh and Geelong forward Jackie Perry. Sydney racked up nine wins, a club record.

“It’s a good catapult ... into the finals, close wins like that,” Molloy told Fox Footy.

“It always brings out a bit extra energy, especially when you hear Wharfie Time.”

Geelong will host Melbourne, followed by reigning premiers North Melbourne against Carlton in a qualifying-final double header next Saturday afternoon at Ikon Park.

Sydney expect to pack out Henson Park on Sunday against the Bulldogs, before Gold Coast host Hawthorn in the other elimination final.

text:

Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election Airport rail study doctored to ‘bake-in’ Sunshine as preferred route, commission told Chip Le Grand Updated November 2, 2026 — 3:03pm ,first published November 2, 2026 — 5:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. State Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has urged the Big Build royal commission to fully investigate allegations that former premier Jacinta Allan coerced public servants to back her government’s plans for the Melbourne Airport Rail Project. But Wilson said that if the Coalition government is elected, the project would continue as designed. Jacinta Allan, pictured next to Daniel Andrews, announces Sunshine as the preferred route for the Melbourne Airport Rail Link before the 2018 election. Paul Jeffers This masthead on Monday reported allegations before the royal commission that financial estimates were doctored, and a senior public servant was threatened with the sack to ensure the proposed MARL ran through Sunshine instead of a more direct route to the city. The allegations challenge the integrity of the business case for Premier Ben Carroll’s priority project, call into question a $12 billion joint funding commitment by the state and federal governments, and plunge the Big Build into fresh scandal a month before the state election.

Advertisement

Related Article Victorian election Wilson insists SRL position is ‘very clear’ despite days of confusion Wilson said the royal commission needed to examine the claims. “What we need to get to the bottom of is how, eight years ago, a minister – Jacinta Allan at the time – was intimidating, bullying and threatening public servants to get a political outcome,” she said on Monday. “That is what the royal commission needs to look into.” Pressed on whether a Coalition government would review the project in light of the allegations or consider an alternative route, Wilson said it would be built as planned. “The route is the route. The contracts have been signed, the project is underway and the Coalition is committed to delivering airport rail.”

Advertisement

Allan denies the allegations. She is expected to be called as a witness before the commission. A confidential submission to the royal commission by a planning expert who advised on the airport rail link reveals that a secret working group was established in late 2017 or early 2018 at the direction of then-public transport minister Allan to allegedly bake in the case for the Sunshine route. It says the small group, which included public servants within the Transport Department and outside consultants, was told to not discuss its work with any of their colleagues, including direct reports, or diarise their meetings. All instructions were given verbally. The group’s brief, according to the submission, was to study four shortlisted routes for the Melbourne Airport Rail Link (MARL) and build evidence supporting the state government’s politically favoured outcome – that the new train line, if ever built, would have to go through Sunshine.

Advertisement

“The task was to produce a document, or set of documents, prior to the 2018 election so that after that election there would be no further consideration of any alternative routes for the MARL other than through Sunshine,” the submission reads. Carroll did not address the allegations before the royal commission when questioned by this masthead. On Monday, he cancelled a pre-scheduled press conference. Premier Ben Carroll axed a pre-scheduled press conference on Monday. Louis Trerise “The premier’s first act was to establish the toughest royal commission into the construction industry to leave no stone unturned,” a spokesman said on Sunday. “The terms of reference are broad and expansive. Nothing is off limits. We won’t pre-empt its findings.” Opposition transport infrastructure spokesman Evan Mulholland said Victorians were owed a more substantial response. “Ben Carroll was sitting around the table as a deputy premier and as a senior minister in the government. He needs to explain what he knew and when he knew it.”

Advertisement

The submission from the planing expert is one of four to the royal commission raising concerns about the integrity of the current MARL project. All were provided to this masthead by their respective authors. The most serious allegation raised by the planning expert is that, to make an iron-clad case for Sunshine, the estimated cost of a more direct route through Maribyrnong was intentionally inflated by exaggerating the amount of tunnelling required. And the winner is – Sunshine. The state government announced its preferred route in 2018. Paul Jeffers The Maribyrnong route would have run beneath Highpoint shopping centre and opened up disused defence land for residential development. An earlier 2012 study, commissioned by the then Liberal state government, top-scored Maribyrnong, known at the time as the “direct tunnel” option, out of 22 possible routes, with Sunshine ranked a close second.

Advertisement

The allegation that costings were deliberately inflated to rule Maribyrnong out of contention is contained in a separate, contemporaneous file note made by a solicitor when the planning expert first sought legal advice about blowing the whistle. The note, dated August 23, 2018, and seen by The Age, reads: “Untenable. Serious matters ignored, not acted upon. “4 options – one particular route better but more expensive (doctored to make it unviable).” The solicitor who wrote the file note confirmed its authenticity. The planning expert, who spoke to this masthead on the condition of anonymity, decided against making a disclosure to the Victorian Ombudsman or IBAC due to fears of personal and professional recriminations. They subsequently quit the department, leaving the information buried for eight years.

Advertisement

“This is fraud on a billion-dollar scale,” they said. The planning expert, working with trusted former colleagues experienced in rail engineering and major project costing, has calculated that an unnecessary 3.5 kilometres of tunnelling was included along the proposed Maribyrnong route to add between $3.8 billion and $4.6 billion to the estimated cost. A price tag of $20 billion to $25 billion for Maribyrnong – double the estimated $8 billion to $13 billion cost of the Sunshine route – was included in a strategic appraisal of the airport rail link published by Transport for Victoria in July 2018 and built into the 2021 business case for the project. A truer, average cost estimate of the Maribyrnong route, according to detailed calculations provided to this masthead by the group of experts, is $16.5 billion in 2018 dollars.

Advertisement

Maribyrnong was the federal government’s preferred route when then-prime minister Malcolm Turnbull came to Melbourne in April 2018 to announce $5 billion in funding towards the project. Related Article Public service Thrown in a loop: How Daniel Andrews’ biggest project was cooked up behind closed doors Then-premier Daniel Andrews, who did not appear at the funding announcement alongside Turnbull, was blindsided by the move. At the time, he was more focused on his government’s plans to unveil the Suburban Rail Loop, a project being developed in secret, as a vote-grabbing election promise. The Victorian government formally endorsed the Sunshine route for the airport rail link in August 2018 and the federal government followed suit three months later. The comparative cost of the Maribyrnong route was a critical factor in tipping the scales towards Sunshine in the published assessment. According to the Transport for Victoria analysis, Maribyrnong was the top-scoring route for the benefits it would bring to travellers using the line, Victorian businesses and the economic development of Melbourne’s inner north-west. Due to its prohibitive cost, it was ranked last for deliverability.

Advertisement

When the planning expert saw the assessment, he challenged an executive working in the department. “I just said to him, “How could you produce documents like this, and think this is OK?” the planning expert told this masthead. “He said to me, ‘The minister said to me that either these documents say Sunshine or I’ll sack you. So they say Sunshine.’” Allan, who is retiring from politics after losing the Labor leadership to Carroll in July, was the minister for public transport and major projects at the time the assessment was done. “The allegations made are incorrect,” a spokesman for the former premier said. “Ms Allan will co-operate with the important work of the royal commission. She will answer whatever questions the royal commission has for her about these allegations, but it is not appropriate to pre-empt the royal commission’s work.”

Advertisement

Related Article Analysis

Big Build royal commission Royal commission hints at original sin of Big Build A colleague of Allan, who was unauthorised to publicly discuss the matter, said the former premier was furious at the suggestion she would coerce public servants to support a particular outcome. Allan made no secret during her time as a minister responsible for what became known as the Big Build that she wanted the MARL to run through Sunshine. The benefits of Sunshine, which Allan advocated within government and to her federal counterparts, was that it required no tunnelling, would accelerate Sunshine’s development as a second central business district, and would link the airport line with rail services to regional centres. A former cabinet colleague of Allan’s, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said the former premier was insistent the airport rail line had to run through Sunshine so that people travelling to the airport by train from Ballarat or her home town of Bendigo only needed to change trains once.

Advertisement

In December 2018, when defending the government’s decision not to make public a preliminary business case for the project, Allan hinted at a Sunshine bias. “We’ve released previously ... the strategic assessment of the four alignments, which is really what the preliminary business case was about, looking at those four alignments and giving [state and federal] governments the confidence that Sunshine stacked up the best,” she said. Allan’s confidence in the strategic assessment was not shared by the Victorian Auditor-General’s Office (VAGO). The Big Build royal commission led by Chris Kourakis will begin public hearings next week. Joe Armao A 2022 VAGO report into the quality of government business cases used to support major projects was highly critical of the way that route options for the MARL were assessed, describing the work done as “not sufficiently rigorous” and lacking in transparency. The auditor-general noted that the options assessments “significantly influenced” a state government decision to commit $5 billion to the project and were not “validated or revisited in any depth” before they were included in the published business case.

Advertisement

The airport rail allegations go to the heart of a question that commissioner Chris Kourakis has flagged will be central to his inquiry into the Big Build – whether the state government’s $100 billion infrastructure program was primarily designed to advance the public interest or Labor’s electoral prospects. In his opening address to the inquiry, Kourakis noted that “governments must select and design infrastructure projects around the socioeconomic needs of the Victorian public, and not party political interest”. William McDougall (pictured in 2019) worked on most of the major transport construction projects in Victoria since the late 1990s. Jason South The royal commission is scheduled to hold its first public hearings next week. William McDougall, an independent transport planner who has worked in Britain, the Middle East and on signature Big Build projects including the West Gate Tunnel, North East Link, Suburban Rail Loop and the MARL, has told the commission this is not his experience.

Advertisement

“Throughout my career, I have seen an accelerating shift away from integrated, evidence-based planning towards politically selected and prioritised projects,” he writes in a submission provided to this masthead. “The most egregious issue of all is that large projects are chosen for political reasons, announced and funded without the context of an integrated land use and transport plan.” Premier Ben Carroll, pictured with Anthony Albanese near Sunshine, has declared the MARL his “highest priority”. Jason South McDougall, who is aware of the allegations about the development of the MARL now before the royal commission, believes the project is a case study of where Victoria’s planning for and delivery of major transport projects has gone wrong. “A strategic assessment of options … was used to justify the Sunshine/Albion route, but it was a highly skewed assessment with direct, political interference aimed at ensuring that the Sunshine route was the best,” he writes in his submission. “Faster, shorter and cheaper routes were rejected.”

Advertisement

Two further submissions to the royal commission, both made confidentially by former public servants, question the planning process and decisions taken that resulted in Sunshine being chosen as the route for a new airport line. Carroll, since becoming Labor leader, has declared the airport rail link his “highest priority” major project. The government has selected a preferred bidder to redevelop Sunshine station, and Carroll last month was alongside Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to announce forward plans to lay down airport rail tracks to a proposed new station in Keilor East, in the middle of his electorate of Niddrie. The Victorian Coalition has also backed the MARL. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has promised to deliver the project, including a new station at Keilor East, if she becomes Victoria’s next premier. Both the Maribyrnong and Sunshine routes run through Keilor East. Wilson has promised to expand the royal commission’s terms of reference so that it examines whether “any project was conceived, selected, prioritised, expanded, re-scoped, funded or continued, wholly or partly, to confer an industrial, financial, organisational or political benefit” to a trade union or political party.

Accelerate Resources has called in the nation’s top scientific minds, partnering with the government research organisation CSIRO to crack the metallurgical code of its Woodie Woodie North manganese project in Western Australia’s prolific Pilbara region. The company has been awarded a $50,000 Kick-Start research grant, which will fund a detailed characterisation study on its manganese mineralisation – a critical step in designing an effective processing flowsheet and assessing the potential for a saleable product. Large-diameter metallurgical drill core from Accelerate Resources’ Woodie Woodie North project, now at CSIRO’s Perth laboratory for detailed analysis. The study, titled Multiscale Characterisation of Manganese Mineralisation, is to be led by CSIRO’s Dr Yoram Teitler and will analyse 150 metres of large-diameter diamond core from the Dale’s Patch and Nathan’s Flat prospects within the project’s Area 42 deposit. In the first stage, CSIRO will log and scan the core for manganese and associated elements using X-ray fluorescence (XRF) and hyperspectral techniques, while measuring hardness. The second stage will involve petrographic, mineralogical and microanalytical work on representative samples to examine how each mineralisation style formed and how subsequent weathering may have altered their characteristics.

Advertisement

‘CSIRO brings world class mineral characterisation capability to understand how the different manganese ore types behave and give us a much sharper picture of the upgrade potential.’ Accelerate Resources chief executive officer Luke Meter The analysis will help explain how different types of manganese mineralisation respond to processing, while guiding the company’s ongoing metallurgical and ore-sorting testwork. The findings are also expected to sharpen Accelerate’s geological understanding of the deposit, helping inform future resource evaluation and mine planning. Accelerate Resources chief executive officer Luke Meter said: “CSIRO brings world class mineral characterisation capability that would be very difficult for a company of our size to access on this scale. Understanding how the different manganese ore types at Area 42 behave is fundamental to designing the right processing route.” With the core already delivered to CSIRO’s Kensington laboratory in Perth, work is expected to begin shortly. The study is due to finish in mid-2027, when CSIRO will deliver a technical report and recommendations for further work. Accelerate will report its own metallurgical and ore-sorting results as they become available. Woodie Woodie North covers 432 square kilometres, 55km north of Consolidated Minerals’ operating Woodie Woodie manganese mine, in a region known for high-grade manganese. The commodity is on Australia’s Critical Minerals List for its essential role in steelmaking and growing use in lithium-ion battery chemistries.

Advertisement

Accelerate has already defined a maiden inferred resource of 1.2 million tonnes grading a respectable 19.1 per cent manganese and has outlined a much larger conceptual exploration target of between 5.3 million and 10.7 million tonnes at 10 to 19 per cent manganese. Neither includes the company’s Gingarrigan and El Largo trends. These high-grade corridors sit beyond both figures and emerged throughrecent mapping of more than 200 manganese outcrops across Woodie Woodie North. Rock chips returned up to 59.4 per cent manganese at El Largo, 12km south-east of Area 42, and 59.6 per cent at the separate Faris prospect 2km south-east of the resource. The surface grades flag the potential for a simple direct-shipping-ore (DSO) operation down the track, subject to further drilling and metallurgical tests. While drilling is ongoing across the project, the core being studied comes from earlier large-diameter work at Area 42, where Accelerate reported visual manganese across a 72-metre downhole span at Nathan’s Flat in October, from 5.6m to the end of the hole at 77.6m. The CSIRO collaboration adds another dimension to Accelerate’s manganese ambitions at Woodie Woodie North, which sits alongside its gold projects in WA’s Eastern Goldfields at Balagundi and Kanowna East, and lithium prospects near Karratha. For a junior explorer, leveraging CSIRO’s world-class firepower is a serious coup. Getting the metallurgy right is often the key that unlocks a project’s value, and by decoding its ore, Accelerate could be fast-tracking its path from Pilbara explorer to producer. title: America's comeback story? These voters aren't so sure
text:
IN BRIEF US voters will have their say in the midterm elections amid tough economic conditions.

Some say Trump has failed to deliver on economic renewal.

In 1982, singer Billy Joel wrote a line that's still painfully true for these voters in the United States.

"We're living here in Allentown and they're closing all the factories down."

More than four decades later, Pennsylvania's Lehigh Valley, where Allentown sits, is grappling with the decline of its manufacturing industry and its once firmly blue-collar identity.

"It's pretty much gone," Joe Nemeth, a former Bethlehem Steel worker, tells SBS News.

"It used to be a very working-class town. Lot of hard-working people. And I can't say that's true anymore."

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Born and raised in Allentown, Nemeth followed in the footsteps of his grandfather, working at Bethlehem Steel before its last operating blast furnace went cold in 1995.

The plant that once supplied steel for landmarks including the Empire State Building and the Golden Gate Bridge has been transformed into an arts space, but for some, the towering smokestacks are a harsh reminder of the economic decline.

That decline helped turn the Lehigh Valley into a political battleground ahead of the midterm elections, with its competitive House races potentially pivotal to the Democrats' bid to regain control of Congress.

Here, promises of economic revival are closely scrutinised.

The ruins of the former Bethlehem Steel Corporation loom large over the town that grew around the industrial giant, a reminder of the the area's once thriving industrial economy and identity. Source: SBS News / Alexandra Jones

On 2 April 2025, the so-called Liberation Day when US President Donald Trump announced sweeping tariffs, he promised that jobs and factories would "come roaring back" to the US.

In the months that followed, US manufacturing shed 82,000 jobs, according to the country's Bureau of Labor Statistics.

It has since recovered 72,000 jobs as of September this year, still leaving a 21,000-job deficit from the start of Trump's second term in January 2025, according to the Economic Policy Institute.

Molten iron is poured during a demonstration at the annual Steel Weekend event celebrating Bethlehem's steelmaking heritage and the industrial traditions that shaped the region. Source: SBS News / Alexandra Jones

Mack Truck employees fear for the future of jobs

While Bethlehem Steel has been consigned to history, another iconic US manufacturer, Mack Trucks, still operates a facility in the Lehigh Valley’s Lower Macungie township.

Founded in the US in 1900, the company has been owned by Sweden's Volvo Group since 2000.

Michael Shupp, president of United Auto Workers Local 677, the union representing Mack Trucks workers, says manufacturing was once the beating heart of the Lehigh Valley.

"Between Mack Trucks and Bethlehem Steel, if you didn't have a family member that was working in one of those two facilities, you hadn't been here long," he tells SBS News.

Michael Shupp, president of UAW Local 677, says workers remain concerned about job security and the future of manufacturing as economic pressures continue to affect industrial communities. Source: SBS News / Alexandra Jones

Today, the facility employs more than 2,000 people, but its role has shifted to final assembly and customisation, with components sourced from elsewhere.

"This whole culture of trying to find things cheaper and better, it destroyed the Lehigh Valley for a generation of families," Shupp says.

While he says promises of more jobs may have been kept, he questions whether those jobs offer a sustainable livelihood.

"We have been given the same promise as the rest of the country, that we're going to have more jobs, the jobs are going to be better."

READ MORE What comes after Trump? The bigger battle behind the US midterms

"Those jobs are relying on government subsidies to support the workers, whether they’re on Medicaid, whether they're on food stamps. Those jobs are not paying a living wage."

And with a new Mack Trucks facility opening in Monterrey, Mexico, Shupp says there's fresh anxiety at the Pennsylvania plant.

While there's uncertainty and a lack of transparency about what the Mexico facility will produce, its contract guarantees the Macungie facility will build the majority of the trucks. But the volume of trucks that could be outsourced would still be significant.

Shawn Smith (left) and his daughter Sabrina both work at Mack Trucks. Both generations are concerned about the future of American manufacturing jobs. Source: SBS News / Alexandra Jones

For Mack Trucks employee Sabrina Smith, who works with her father on the factory floor, there are growing questions about job security, and a feeling wages simply aren't fair.

"There are some people saying, 'Well, [the Mexico factory is] bigger than we thought it would be.' Or that the cost going into it was a little more than they said initially," Smith says.

Shupp says problems for workers began with the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), signed in 1992 and implemented in 1994.

"I can't blame Trump because he's just been the last person responsible for letting us down," he says.

Critics argue it accelerated the decline of the automotive industry by increasing movement of production across borders.

A UAW publication on trade policy and manufacturing jobs highlights ongoing debate over the impact of NAFTA and the United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement (USMCA), on American workers and industrial communities. Source: SBS News / Alexandra Jones

Sabrina's father Shawn says unkept promises over decades have fractured the union base and shifted political allegiances.

"My first election was 1992, and I voted for Bill Clinton. I look at what he did with NAFTA and that was really the start of the downfall of the automotive industry," he says.

The Macungie Mack Trucks facility has been regularly visited by presidents both red and blue.

Joe Biden visited in 2021, attempting to promote US manufacturing jobs.

But Smith says when Trump visited in June, "it turned into a Republican rally".

"The agreement to have him in was to be promoting Mack Trucks' 125 years and we're going for military contracts and all this other stuff. But then the whole thing ended up being like a political rally and that rubbed a lot of people the wrong way."

Historic photographs of Mack Trucks workers at UAW Local 677 headquarters document decades of worker activism. Source: SBS News / Alexandra Jones

Mike Dzwonczyk is the former treasurer of the Steelworkers union, which he says was once the "most powerful union in the state".

He says the lack of blue-collar jobs is just one factor that's led union members to vote Republican in the past.

"The rank and file [in the unions] are switching to Republicans. Sad to say," Dzwonczyk says.

But whether they'll stay red this time is in doubt, Smith says.

Mike Dzwonczyk spent decades working in the blast furnaces of Bethlehem Steel. Source: SBS News / Alexandra Jones

Farmers hit by tariffs

Pennsylvania's farmers were also hit hard by tariffs.

Seventh-generation farmer Kevin Witmer, who produces a diverse range of crops and livestock in Lancaster County, voted for Trump three times.

But he says tariffs have had "no positives" for his business.

His soybean exports have been hit hardest as Chinese interest dropped off due to higher costs.

"If China doesn't buy, it definitely affects the prices. It's a global market," Witmer tells SBS News.

According to the US department of agriculture, US soybean exports to China dropped from 26.8 million tonnes in 2024 to 7.2 million tonnes in 2025 — a 73 per cent decline.

Alongside corn, wheat and soybeans, Kevin Witmer grows tobacco for the cigar industry, one of the region's earliest commercial crops. Witmer says "America was built on tobacco money". Source: SBS News / Alexandra Jones

Witmer is also contending with soaring fuel and fertiliser costs stemming from the Iran war. Less money is coming in and more is going out.

"The fuel cost is crazy. I don't see it going down anytime soon," he says.

"It just wrecked my budget. I was selling corn with the idea that fertiliser was going to be, say, $300 [USD] a ton, and two weeks later all of a sudden it's $400, $500, $600 a ton."

Immigration policies taking an economic toll

Further east is Kennett Square, the mushroom capital of the world.

The local mushroom industry contributed nearly $US4 billion ($5.6 billion) to the local economy according to a 2022 estimate.

Third-generation mushroom farmer Chris Alonzo says on top of tariffs and rising input costs, immigration policy is also compounding workforce shortages.

Third-generation mushroom farmer Chris Alonzo says the combined pressures of tariffs and rising living costs have hurt demand for mushrooms. In response, he has diversified his business, producing vegan bacon made from mycelium. Source: SBS News / Alexandra Jones

The industry relies almost exclusively on migrant labour.

"We just don't have enough workers in the industry to harvest the mushrooms, to do packing, to do all the tasks."

While there have not been major immigration enforcement activities in the area, Alonzo says uncertainty and anti-migrant rhetoric are taking a toll.

"The fear is worse than the actual raids."

With the economic fallout being felt in farming and blue-collar communities around the country, it's raising questions about whether Trump and the Republicans will be punished at the midterms.

title: Superannuation watchdog warns widespread complaints signal industry 'failures'
text:
IN BRIEF The watchdog found 25 per cent of super funds weren't analysing customer complaints data to identify systemic issues.

Experts warn it's a concerning sign of customer and complaints culture, and risk culture across the industry.

Superannuation funds are ignoring warning signs as complaints about the way they treat customers mount, the corporate watchdog says.

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) has found superannuation funds wanting in handling members' complaints at a critical time for the $3.4 trillion industry.

As millions of Australians transition from accumulating super balances to withdrawing their retirement income, issues such as timely payment of death benefits have been piling up.

Commissioner Simone Constant said super funds should treat complaints as the "canary in the coal mine", but were often ignoring the warning signs.

"Superannuation is too important for there to be failures now, in terms of member services and complaints," she told the Australian Associated Press.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The death benefit failures were an example of how better complaints-handling could have saved members and their families from harm, the regulator found in a report released on Monday.

The regulator has been cracking down on the industry after finding widespread delays in trustees paying out deceased customers' remaining super balances and insurance payments to family members.

In some cases, loved ones waited years to receive money they were owed.

The regulator reviewed all 45 superannuation trustees and found a quarter were not regularly analysing their complaints data to identify systemic issues, Constant said.

That comes despite a 43 per cent year-on-year increase in superannuation complaints to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA).

READ MORE Which super funds earned a retirement tick of approval?

Constant said the issue was industry-wide, declining to single out any particular funds for poor complaints handling.

"We see some funds detecting zero or practically zero systemic issues from complaints, despite AFCA identifying complaints [that could be systemic] at twice the rate of the industry," she said.

While complaints growth flattened for a period after the death benefits issues were identified, the regulator has seen it rising again.

That raised real concerns about customer culture, complaints culture, and risk culture across the industry, Constant said.

"When we see several of the funds attributing well more than half of the root causes to the customers, essentially blaming the customer, we're really concerned about whether the industry has used the time, used the processes, and used their complaints data to understand what's really going on with their members in terms of these important services," she said.

READ MORE There's another reason to check who inherits your superannuation

The Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia said the industry heard loud and clear that trustees needed to do better.

"There are clear areas for improvement here, and the sector will use the information ASIC has collected and its recommendations to act quickly to better use complaints to improve how we look after members," the association's chief executive Mary Delahunty said.

"Members reasonably expect super funds to listen to them, and this should be uniform across the industry."

title: Sydney housing market has reached a new low. But are homes affordable?
text:
IN BRIEF The national home price slump has dropped 6.7 per cent since the March peak, according to new data.

Experts warn buyers seeking affordability may have to wait for prices to fall further, or for interest rate cuts.

Sydney home prices are lower than they were five years ago but Australia's housing downturn has a way to go to return to affordable values.

National median dwelling values fell another 1.2 per cent in October, extending the home price slump to 6.7 per cent since the March peak, data provider Cotality reported on Monday.

In a market already constrained by elevated affordability and serviceability pressures, rising interest rates and higher taxes have further weighed on housing demand.

In Sydney, the market that led the downturn, prices fell 1.6 per cent in the month.

At $1,178,959, the median Sydney dwelling is more than 10 per cent cheaper than the February peak and has dropped below where it was five years ago.

But the mid-sized capitals of Perth and Brisbane are falling even faster.

"We saw such an enormous accumulation of value in those mid-sized capitals over the past five years," Cotality head of research Gerard Burg said.

"It means when you see these sizeable declines in those markets, they have a lot they can give up, with a lot of homeowners not feeling too much direct pain."

Brisbane's median value plunged two per cent in October but was still 46 per cent more expensive than five years earlier.

In Perth, where prices were growing at an annual rate of about 25 per cent a few months ago, values fell 1.7 per cent.

In Melbourne, it was a very different story, Burg said.

The Victorian capital has underperformed the rest of the country for five years but is now giving up value more slowly than the other mainland capitals.

Melbourne's affordability advantage was starting to attract residents on net, a reversal from the exodus to cities like Perth and Brisbane during the COVID-19 pandemic, Burg said.

Still, Melbourne-based Ray White real estate agent Dexter Prack says the declines are the biggest he has witnessed in his 28-year career.

"Some properties, they've gone back to 2017, 2018 prices, which is scary," he told the Australian Associated Press.

In the prestige Mornington Peninsula market, Prack said some properties were going on the market at a 25 per cent discount.

By exiting a falling market, some investors would have taken a sizeable haircut. But for owner-occupier vendors buying in a falling market, Prack said there were plenty of opportunities.

However, prospective buyers would have to wait for prices to fall further, or for the Reserve Bank to start cutting interest rates, to see affordability really improve.

Nationally, the median dwelling value is worth approximately $63,400 less than in March.

Four interest rate rises have eroded a median household's borrowing capacity by about $71,000 since February, Burg said.

The Reserve Bank is widely tipped to hike rates again on Tuesday.

With most economists not forecasting a cut until late 2027, Burg expects values to keep falling until then.

title: Why this Native American nation is taking on Donald Trump
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

At the heart of the Sonoran Desert in southern Arizona, a great green sea unfolds between sky islands, bringing unexpected lushness to an otherwise arid landscape.

Thousands of towering saguaro cacti and fanned fronds of ocotillo rise from the dusty earth, while a road tracing the United States-Mexico border stretches as far as the eye can see.

This is part of the Tohono O'odham Nation, a federally recognised Native American nation whose reservation, the second-largest in Arizona, spans 1.1 million hectares.

Its leaders are fighting plans by the Trump administration to build a 9m steel border wall along part of their boundary with Mexico, arguing it would divide their lands, threaten sacred sites and further disrupt a community whose cultural and family ties span both sides of the border.

Tohono O'odham Nation leaders are fighting against the Trump administration's plans. Source: SBS News

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The government, meanwhile, argues that the wall is necessary to strengthen border security.

Of the Nation's approximately 37,000 registered members, around 12,000 live on the reservation and 3,000 live across the border in the Mexican state of Sonora.

The Tohono O'odham – meaning 'desert people' — have been the traditional custodians of this area for more than 10,000 years, with ancestral lands reaching far beyond the boundaries of the present-day reservation.

The Nation's chair, Verlon Jose, remembers a time when there was no concept of a border.

"I used to travel with my dad or my grandfather; we would go across a fence line. I never knew we were going into another country," he tells SBS News.

"All I knew was we were going to the community, to help grandma and grandpa or go to some event."

Verlon Jose remembers a time when there was no concept of a border. Source: SBS News / Alexandra Jones

Like many others on the reservation, Jose grew up on a cattle ranch.

"I was riding horses before I even learned how to walk. My dad was a cowboy. We were always working the land," he says.

"That's how it was growing up, lot of hard work, a lot of family time … a lot of culture and tradition shared, a lot of singing, dancing."

Jose says the Nation has worked with the federal government for decades to address drug trafficking, unauthorised migration and cartel activity across the border.

He says the Nation's opposition to the proposed wall does not mean it opposes border security.

"I've seen from no barrier, to a fence barrier, to a vehicle barrier," Jose says, pointing to the barbed-wire fence and the dark, rusty-red, approximately 1m-high steel barricades known as "Normandy-style", installed nearly 20 years ago to stop vehicles crossing the border.

In recent months, the Nation has restricted access for outside visitors as it disputes the federal government's plans to build a pedestrian wall along about 100km of its international boundary with Mexico.

From Sells, the Nation's capital, the road stretches south to the Mexican border.

"See these plants here, they are tagged for removal," Jose says, showing us.

Small white tags hang from protected ocotillo and saguaro cacti along the border line. Jose says the plants are marked for removal and relocation to make way for construction.

Thousands of metal tags hang on ocotillo and saguaro near the border line. Source: SBS News / Alexandra Jones

The saguaro — Ha-San in the Tohono language — is sacred and was granted legal personhood by the Nation's legislative council in 2021.

"In our culture, in our history, is that the saguaro came from a child," Jose says.

"When I look at the saguaro out here, these are our people that have been here for hundreds of years."

The success of them surviving any movement to be transplanted anywhere else is very low.

"Would you like for me to go up and uproot your child … and send them on a path for destruction, to their deathbed? Because when we remove those, that's what we're doing."

Saguaro cacti are sacred to the Tohono O'odham, and some that are hundreds of years old have been tagged for removal and relocation to make way for a border wall. Source: SBS News / Alexandra Jones

Jose believes the push to accelerate construction is politically motivated, arguing that the administration is seeking to drum up support among US President Donald Trump's political base ahead of the midterm elections.

This is Trump's wall. This is not America's wall.

"The Trump administration is doing everything in their effort to expedite to make a political statement here.

"They say, 'We recognise the nation as a sovereign nation'. If you are, then let us protect our land."

The legal battle

In June, the Nation filed a lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to stop construction. It argued that the wall would infringe on its sovereignty, threaten wildlife movement and put the Nation's fiercely guarded water resources at risk.

In August, a federal judge in Washington, DC rejected the Nation's request for an injunction to halt the project.

At the heart of the dispute is the Roosevelt Reservation, a federally designated strip of land along the border. The government maintains it has the authority to build barriers there, while the Nation argues that contractors would have to cross tribal lands to access the border strip, which would constitute trespass.

The Nation is appealing the ruling, citing a sharp decline in unauthorised crossings and arguing that its cooperation with law enforcement has improved border security.

The Trump administration argues that stretches of the border without a pedestrian barrier remain vulnerable, particularly as new sections of wall are built elsewhere.

The protected and native ocotillo grows metres tall; thousands have also been tagged for removal. Source: SBS News / Alexandra Jones

Construction of new border wall sections has ramped up in recent months, including in Texas, New Mexico, and other parts of Arizona.

In nearby Lochiel, construction has begun on a double wall parallel to the existing barrier. There, protesters have clashed with authorities over the removal of so-called "grandmother trees".

Opponents of the construction have also raised concerns about damage to sacred sites and culturally significant landscapes.

In April, DHS contractors bulldozed part of the Las Playas Intaglio, an ancient, fish-shaped carving scraped into the earth, estimated to be at least 6,500 years old, in a separate border-wall construction area west of the Tohono O'odham reservation.

Along this line that they call the international border, there are secret areas. There are places of worship. There are places of prayer.

"There are human remains along here that would be destroyed," Jose says.

Cross-border ties

A protest camp has been established at the San Miguel gate since August.

For community members, the dispute goes beyond the proposed wall. Nation member Davey Cross says crossing the border has already become increasingly difficult, even without the new barrier.

He says people who want to pass must press a button and wait for border patrol agents to unlock it.

Members of the Tohono O'odham Nation established the Tadai Me:i Prayer Camp at the San Miguel Gate along the US-Mexico border as a protest against planned wall construction. Source: SBS News / Alexandra Jones

"Before, there used to be people right here at the trees and there's a lady that came and set up and she sell, you know, tacos, burritos, whatever. And other people would come with fruit and jewellery, and sell to everybody," Cross tells SBS News.

It was like a market right there. Now ... you have to wait for border patrol to open this and then they get your IDs and run you for felony warrants.

The dispute is also drawing support from Indigenous communities and others beyond the reservation.

Church leaders from several denominations have spoken out against the wall, including at a rally on the San Xavier Reservation, a northern district of the Tohono O'odham Nation.

At the event earlier this month, a nation member, Lorraine Juan, described the emotional toll the plans are taking on the community.

"The people that are building this wall don't care that they're desecrating our land, our ancestors," Juan says, holding back tears.

The saguaros, they're killing them. Those are our ancestors. I hope that and pray that this wall stops. It's only hurting us, hurting the land, hurting the animals and hurting our people.

With the midterms on 3 November, Nation leaders are encouraging members to turn out to vote. Native Americans were granted the right to vote in Arizona in 1948, but many continued to face barriers for decades. It was only in 1972, when the state repealed its English-language literacy test, that one of the most significant hurdles was lifted.

Nation vice chair Carla Johnson tells SBS News: "It is within our lifetime that people could remember when they didn't have the right to vote.

"The Indigenous people, the first people here, did not have that right to vote. And now we do."

The Native American vote can be influential when it turns out in force. It helped swing Arizona for Joe Biden in 2020.

For Cross, however, the political system has done little to reassure him that the Nation's concerns will be heard. He says he feels little allegiance to either major party.

Nation member Davey Cross says the border is becoming more difficult to cross, even without a new wall. Source: SBS News / Ben Partridge

"Because of everything that's happening. It's sad the way they treat us."

Native American turnout is closely watched in Arizona's tight election, and Jose says Nation leaders have worked hard to ensure members can cast ballots, including arranging transportation to polling stations.

"We want to let the people know that they have a right, that they have a strong voice.

When you say that your vote doesn't count, it does count. Every single vote counts.

title: Why is James Packer testifying at Benjamin Netanyahu's corruption trial?
text:
IN BRIEF James Packer will testify remotely, rejecting a request from Benjamin Netanyahu's lawyer to travel to Israel.

It's alleged a company linked to Packer has made monthly payments to the law firm representing Netanyahu since 2024.

Australian billionaire James Packer has been called to testify at the corruption trial of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu amid reports of secret payments to a Tel Aviv law firm.

According to reporting by The Sydney Morning Herald, Packer paid at least $1.78 million to Hadad Roth Shenhar, the law firm defending Netanyahu against claims that he corruptly received benefits from Packer and other wealthy supporters between 2014 and 2016.

It's alleged that for two years, monthly transfers of over $71,000 were wired from an account under Packer's company, Consolidated Press International, to Hadad Roth Shenhar's account.

Consolidated Press International is one of the several private investment arms operated by Packer. It's alleged the first payment was made on 23 September 2024.

If Packer's alleged investments directly or indirectly benefited Netanyahu, the prime minister could face fresh charges.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

There is no evidence Netanyahu received any benefit from the payments.

SBS News is not suggesting any wrongdoing by Netanyahu, Packer or Hadad Roth Shenhar.

Packer to testify remotely

Netanyahu's primary defence attorney is Amit Hadad, Hadad Roth Shenhar's most senior lawyer.

On 22 October, Hadad contacted Packer and asked him to travel to Israel to testify at the trial. Hadad also extended the request to Packer's associates Ben Tilley and Guy Jalland.

The Sydney Morning Herald published a segment of Packer's response, written on his behalf by Jalland, who was formerly Consolidated Press Holdings CEO.

Jalland said the trio are not prepared to "travel to Israel for that purpose".

The men said they would testify and agreed to appear remotely via audiovisual link.

READ MORE Israeli president to begin coalition talks in hopes of finding path to government

Jallad confirmed that he and Tilley had accompanied Packer on "a number of visits to Israel in the period of 2013 to 2016". Neither man is accused of wrongdoing.

It is yet to be determined where Packer will give evidence.

In the letter, Hadad denied Packer's investments are related to Netanyahu's trial — saying Hadad Roth Shenhar represented companies controlled by Packer on other matters.

Packer is yet to comment.

A history of friendship

In February 2018, the Israeli Police named Packer in connection with the bribery and fraud allegations against Netanyahu.

The Australian Federal Police interviewed him as a witness on behalf of their Israeli counterparts the year before.

The Israeli police recommended that the attorney-general indict Netanyahu — who denied all wrongdoing and dismissed rumours that he would resign as prime minister.

READ MORE Netanyahu bloc narrowly ahead as Israeli PM claims Arab parties gained from voter fraud

Packer was linked to Netanyahu's corruption case after allegations that he gifted the politician cigars and champagne sometime between 2014 and 2016.

At the time, Packer and Netanyahu were neighbours, both residing in luxury private villas in Caesarea, on Israel's Mediterranean coast.

However, the pair became estranged in 2016 after the corruption allegations were levelled against Netanyahu.

They were not spotted together again until July 2024, when Packer attended Netanyahu's US Congress address. He would later attend Netanyahu's UN General Assembly address in New York in September the same year.

Australian billionaire James Packer attended Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's speech to the US Congress in July 2024. Source: AFP / Drew Angerer

Packer is the son of the late Australian media mogul Kerry Packer.

The 59-year-old inherited the family fortune after his father died in 2005 and has a net worth of more than $5.2 billion according to Forbes.

title: 'No area exempt': Nothing off limits as Labor hunts for savings ahead of RBA meeting
text:
In brief Labor has signalled that no area of government spending will be exempt as it searches for budget savings.

Persistent inflation has fuelled expectations that the Reserve Bank will once again raise interest rates.

Nowhere will be off limits for the razor gang while Labor searches for savings as it faces heat for still-rising inflation.

Persistently fast-rising prices have fuelled criticism of high public spending after inflation came in hotter than expected in the year to September.

Accelerating inflation has driven expectations that the Reserve Bank will on Tuesday hike the cash rate to its highest rate in 18 years, pouring more pain on borrowers.

While the Middle East oil shock and ballooning artificial intelligence investment are delivering price pressures largely outside Canberra's control, Labor has also been implored to tighten its belt in December's mid-year budget update.

"I would not say that any area is exempt," Finance Minister Katy Gallagher told ABC's Insiders program on Sunday.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"I'm not saying it's too difficult, but I am saying that there should be some acknowledgement of the world in which we are living and the pressures on the commonwealth budget.

"They are real, they are increasing, and we have to deal with them ... there's a lot of work going into the saving side."

Inflation and government spending

Federal government spending as a percentage of GDP hit 26.9 per cent in the 2025/26 financial year, the highest proportion in four decades outside the COVID-19 pandemic.

The RBA's preferred inflation measure — quarterly trimmed mean — beat the central bank's 0.8 per cent forecast to land at 1 per cent in September.

Headline annual inflation came in at 4.3 per cent, slightly above the consensus estimate.

The result dramatically increased the odds of another interest rate hike on Melbourne Cup day as inflation tracks well outside the RBA's 2-3 per cent target band.

Gallagher described as "overblown" reports of tension between Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Treasurer Jim Chalmers over plans the latter had put forward to find budget savings.

On a Nine podcast appearance during the week, the treasurer said he took responsibility for "difficult things in my portfolio", and he would leave it for other ministers to take responsibility for spending on their patches.

Gallagher said Chalmers was simply "putting up his hand for the role that he plays in the decisions around the budget", which was the result of collective cabinet efforts.

While there were "robust discussions" about budget measures, the Labor frontbencher added the treasurer and prime minister had "a very professional and respectful relationship".

"We've all got slightly different jobs and come at things from slightly different perspectives," she said.

Gallagher defends tax breaks, subsidies

The finance minister defended spending on tax breaks for electric vehicles and generous subsidies for home batteries despite the costs of both schemes blowing out amid higher-than-expected demand.

Their uptake by high income-earners has led to suggestions they amount to middle-class welfare, inviting calls for means-testing.

But Gallagher said the same schemes supported other government priorities, such as the renewable energy transition and electrification of the economy.

"Some of the data is showing that this is helping people on the outskirts of cities and in regional areas with some of those cost-of-living pressures and bringing their energy bills down," she said.

Labor has capped the value of EVs eligible for tax breaks and tightened the battery rebate program, but the cost of that scheme has still blown out to $7.2 billion over four years — more than three times its originally forecast cost.
