title: Rebecca waited more than a decade for housing. Her town fears what's coming next
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

For the past three months, Rebecca Williams has been living in a storage yard without power on the fringes of Far North Queensland.

A broad tarp covers her belongings, and at night she sleeps in a pink swag, which she says offers little shelter from the weather and the noise of trucks hurtling down the nearby highway.

The site also has no toilet.

"None of this is secured, so some nights I feel very unsafe," she tells SBS News.

Her makeshift home sits on the outskirts of Seisia, a small coastal town of around 300 people on the Cape York Peninsula. Rising costs and encroaching seas have created a perfect storm for residents, who are struggling to access affordable and climate-resilient housing.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Williams, 35, is a proud Angkamuthi Seven Rivers woman and works full-time in environmental protection. She says she has been living in "survival mode" for far longer than she’s called the compound home.

She's been waiting for a rental for more than 11 years.

Rebecca Williams is one of around 100 Seisia residents waiting for a long-term rental. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

"I've been told it's based on not having kids. I'm not a priority," she says.

A chronic housing shortage has gripped the community for more than a decade, driven by undersupply, prohibitively high construction costs and overcrowding. Many in the community have no choice but to rely on government-funded housing stock.

While the Queensland Department of Housing is ultimately responsible for social housing across the state, Seisia's local applications are processed by the Northern Peninsula Area Regional Council (NPARC), which also delivers and maintains government-supported homes. But the waitlist is long, forcing some community members to consider leaving their ancestral homeland.

After a decade of couch surfing, living in overcrowded family homes and even taking jobs on boats for two years, Williams moved into her family’s storage yard in June.

The pink swag Rebecca Williams has been sleeping in for the past few months, while awaiting an outcome on her rental application. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

As SBS News was preparing to publish this story, Williams received confirmation from the Department of Housing that it would provide her with emergency accommodation. She expects to move into a government-supported two-bedroom rental with her younger sister in the coming weeks.

She estimates around 100 people in Cape York's Indigenous community are currently waiting for a house — that’s around one in three residents.

"There's a whole heap of us. We're being told to move down to Cairns, but people who are from here, we haven't imagined ourselves living anywhere else," she says.

I see it as structural violence. Maybe a bit of racial, but more structural violence, with not just my generation, but many generations of my family.

A housing crisis on two fronts

Across the Cape York Peninsula, communities like Seisia face similar housing challenges.

As the climate warms and sea levels rise, they are contending with another major threat to their way of life.

Roughly 1,000km north of Cairns, Cape York is bordered by the Coral Sea to the east, the Gulf of Carpentaria to the west and the Torres Strait to the north. Its low-lying, tropical landscape is carved by 21 major river systems, making it home to one of the largest freshwater networks in the country.

Much like the broader Torres Strait region, its topography makes it particularly vulnerable to coastal erosion.

Low-lying coastal areas in Cape York and the surrounding Torres Strait region are at high risk of coastal erosion and flooding events due to climate change. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

It's difficult to predict exactly how much sea-level rise will inundate low-lying areas around the Torres Strait, but the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has identified the region as among the most vulnerable places in the world.

A sea-level rise of just 50cm could make flooding across Australia 300 times more likely, according to the Australian government. By this estimate, a flood that once struck every hundred years would be expected several times a year.

This is a source of deep concern for residents of Cape York, who have witnessed the long-term impacts of flood events and seen First Nations communities displaced.

Sitting on the shores of Seisia Beach, Torres Strait Islander Elders Leonora Adidi and Jenson Warusam recall the "difficult decision" their grandparents made to leave their home in Saibai, a low-lying island in the Torres Strait just a few kilometres off the Papua New Guinea mainland, to establish a new community on the northernmost tip of Australia.

"This was a community that was built by the blood, sweat and tears of our people," Adidi tells SBS News.

Torres Strait Islander Elders Leonora Adidi and Jenson Warusam are among the descendants of the first wave of climate migrants from Saibai. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

The catalyst was a major flooding event, explains Adidi, who is also a linguist and cultural educator from the Suy-Baydham Clan of Bamaga and Saibai.

In 1947, unnatural king tides and heavy monsoon rains struck Saibai, flooding the entire village.

"There wasn't enough fresh water and also fresh food from the gardens to sustain the population," says Adidi, a linguist and cultural educator from the Suy-Baydham Clan of Bamaga and Saibai.

Sabai's chief, Bamaga Ginau, proposed a bold relocation idea.

Source: SBS News

"He put forward his plans that we should all move out and abandon the island," Warusam says.

The community was split: some wanted to leave, while others chose to stay.

Seven families representing seven clan groups sailed south to Cape York in pearl luggers, the M.V. Millard and M.V. Macoy, and established a temporary settlement in the abandoned army camps at Muttee Heads, on Cape York’s west coast. In 1948, the Queensland Government gazetted 44,500 acres (18,008 hectares) as a reserve for Torres Strait Islanders.

More families followed, clearing land and building new houses, until the settlements were renamed Seisia and Bamaga.

This photo, taken in June 1931, shows a dauarti canoe belonging to the Bamaga family, one of the seven Saibai families to migrate permanently to Cape York after 1947. Source: Supplied / Queensland State Archives

"When my grandparents moved here, there was a freak tide, probably due to some underwater event," Adidi says.

In The World's News, a discontinued newspaper formerly published in Sydney, a 1952 headline reads: "Disappearing Island Defies Science", referencing the unnatural tides that inundated Saibai.

But Adidi fears that a one-off event is becoming alarmingly regular.

"It's now getting closer and going into areas where they've never been affected by salt water," she adds.

History repeating itself

While the term climate migration is often associated with people moving from disappearing Pacific islands — such as the recent relocation of Tuvalu citizens to Australia — some historians, climate advocates and members of the Cape York community view Saibai's displaced community as Australia's first internal climate migrants.

Today, the Northern Peninsula Area (NPA) of Cape York remains a gateway to the Torres Strait. Residents are deeply connected to their Saibai roots, sharing the same clan groups, cultural knowledge and totemic systems of the crocodile, or Koedal.

Seisia's Indigenous community was established by Saibai migrants nearly 80 years ago, and many retain strong kinship ties to the island. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

But nearly eight decades after the catastrophic floods that displaced several Saibai families, some NPA residents fear history is repeating itself.

As sea levels rise globally and threaten to submerge the island, Cape York’s chronic housing shortage may not support another generation of migrants from Saibai. Now, both NPARC (the local council) and NPA residents are calling for more government funding to accommodate a future wave of families displaced by rising tides.

Some are taking matters into their own hands.

READ MORE Denis watched his ancestral lands be ravaged as a kid. It sparked a major change

In 2021, two Torres Strait Islander elders, Uncle Pabai Pabai and Uncle Paul Kabai, filed a first-of-its-kind negligence case against the federal government, known as the Australian Climate Case. Kabai, who is based in Saibai, argued the government had failed to protect residents against the threat posed by climate change.

Adidi worked as an interpreter for the Federal Court during the case. The hearings took her back to Saibai for the first time in 25 years.

When Torres Strait Islander Elder Leonora Adidi returned to her ancestral homeland, she witnessed firsthand the damage caused by rising levels. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

"Going on Country and being shown the stark, very drastic changes on Saibai was very shocking. I was in tears," she says.

Her grandmother's garden was unrecognisable. The wide beach she remembered from childhood had been whittled down to a narrow strip. The towering coconut and almond trees had disappeared, replaced by mangroves in the saltwater.

It was like I went to a place I'd never been before.

Scientific evidence heard at the Australian Climate Case suggested that islands such as Saibai, which are only 1.5m above sea level in places, could be unlivable by 2050 if global warming continues on its current trajectory.

"It's going to be underwater if nothing is done, and when that happens, the families have got to move somewhere," Adidi says.

"We established these two communities, Bamaga and Seisia, for our people. In the future, if they want to move, there's always going to be a place for them here."

Pressures on the system

However, the community is already buckling under the demand for new homes. In remote Indigenous communities, government housing can be critical in bridging supply gaps, where private development is extremely limited because remote construction is so expensive.

Former NPARC councillor Frances Elu says more funding is vital to solving the housing crisis in the Northern Peninsula Area. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

Frances Elu, a former NPARC councillor, has witnessed Cape York’s overcrowding crisis unfold over many years.

"[The area has become] overpopulated, I guess — well, I don't guess, I see it. You put more people in an environment that will create a crisis for housing," he says.

But with limited government funding and the need for location-specific infrastructure, there are no simple solutions, he says.

"We've got to somehow assist not only Saibai but Torres Strait Islanders and land is another issue," he says.

There's always room for adapting. At the end of the day, we all related if we're talking about Torres Strait [Islanders].

Although Williams looks set to secure housing now, it took numerous applications over more than a decade. Just before her approval, she had appealed to the NPARC by sending letters and photos documenting her living situation.

She worries for other community members still on the waitlist. Relocation is not an option for many who, like Williams, have deep cultural and kinship ties to the region. Saibai is the Country of her ancestors, and her grandparents were among the first wave of climate-displaced migrants to leave the island for the NPA.

"My grandmother was one of the pioneers coming over looking for fresh water. They've worked really hard building these communities," she says.

She believes the government owes the community "a basic duty of care".

Rebecca Williams may have secured social housing, but many others in her community remain in limbo. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

According to NPARC’s analysis of Census data from 2021, 44 per cent of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in the NPA lacked access to appropriately sized housing, and at least 1,385 additional bedrooms were required to relieve overcrowding. According to the council, this would equate to 462 three-bedroom houses.

NPARC has appealed to the federal government for $137 million to reduce chronic overcrowding. Last month, councillors and NPA community leaders travelled to Canberra to urge the government to fund at least 120 new dwellings across the five NPA communities, as well as maintenance for existing houses.

But building houses in a remote area like Cape York is not easy.

Construction materials and skilled contractors are disproportionately costly. According to NPARC's 2024-2025 budget, 15 new homes cost $15 million to build – roughly $1 million each.

A compounding crisis

For now, both councillors and community members alike are awaiting the federal government’s response.

According to a spokesperson for NPARC, there has been no dedicated federal funding to deliver housing for Queensland Indigenous Communities since 2019.

Council has a role in advocating for investments and to work together with the state government to deliver housing on the ground in our community.

Acknowledging the funding "shortfall", NPARC is calling on the federal government to commit $1 billion from the Housing Australia Future Fund to support Queensland's Indigenous communities.

"Overcrowding has measurable consequences for health and education, including transmission of infectious diseases and acute rheumatic fever," the spokesperson says.

SBS News contacted the Queensland Department of Housing and Public Works for comment but did not receive a response before deadline.

Tess Lea, an anthropologist and Head of Macquarie University’s School of Communication, Society and Culture, says funding social housing is particularly challenging in Indigenous communities.

"The who's responsible question at the moment is kind of everyone and no one. There's no single minister or agency with the responsibility for Indigenous housing," Lea tells SBS News.

"You've got many more Indigenous people dependent on social housing than any other population group in Australia."

While nationally, social housing represents a small minority of total housing stock (in 2025, it accounted for just 4 per cent according to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare), much of this problem is structural, Lea explains.

"We've got greater vulnerability [among First Nations communities] just on the basis of the histories of geolocation," she says.

"That's a colonial story – where did water theft start first, where was the most arable land, where was the rich soil."

As sea levels rise, Indigenous communities in and around the Torres Strait are at particular risk of displacement. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

As Indigenous communities have been displaced and forcibly resettled, their vulnerability to climatic and extreme weather events has increased, she explains.

"Australia's at the front lines of climate change," Lea says.

"We're in the age of fire. There's potentially less water or more intense heat events and flooding events."

First Nations communities, she says, are "the collateral … of dragging our feet".

Williams says if another wave of climate migration comes from the Torres Strait islands, she hopes history will not repeat itself, leaving those already displaced from their homelands without access to basic housing.

"We're the people already here, and we're not being looked after," she says.

We're the children of NPA, and we're the homeless children of NPA.

title: What happens when Australia’s inflation basket gets reweighted?
text:
in brief The latest CPI data shows inflation accelerating, with transport, housing and food among key drivers.

The ABS is about to reweight the CPI basket of goods to produce a better measure of inflation.

Last week, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) reported an unexpected spike in inflation in September, prompting fears of more interest rate hikes.

According to the ABS Consumer Price Index (CPI), Australia's annual inflation rate sits at 4.3 per cent — up from 4 per cent in August.

Amongst the largest contributors to rising inflation were housing, which rose 5.2 per cent; alcohol and tobacco, which rose 4.3 per cent and health, which rose 3.7 per cent.

The ABS will be reweighting the CPI basket of goods in January to better reflect current spending trends and produce a more accurate CPI, a crucial exercise as Australians adjust their spending amid continued rising costs.

According to retail expert at the University of Sydney Business School, Lisa Asher, a reweighting exercise is undertaken to "adequately reflect" what people are "actually spending" their money on.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

While a change usually occurs at the end of each year, the ABS had postponed the 2026 change to January. The last reweight was in early 2025.

"Some of the key changes or movements that we saw last year and this year focus much more on the increase in food and non-alcoholic beverages, as a larger percentage, as well as health costs and transport," Asher said.

While the ABS does not flag early what the new weightings may look like, previous changes offer some clues.

In 2025, the biggest weighting increases were in education, health and food and non-alcoholic beverages and the larger weight decreases were in furnishings, household equipment and services, alcohol and tobacco and housing.

What is the CPI and how is calculated?

The CPI is "really a measure of inflation" or "price changes in the economy" and it is based on a representative basket of goods and services for Australian households, head of price statistics at the ABS, Rachael McCririck, said.

The CPI provides a "sense of the underlying price pressures in the economy" but isn't a good measure for how the cost of living crisis is impacting individual households.

"The CPI is really an aggregate measure that informs policymakers and decision-makers about aggregate trends, it informs things like monetary and fiscal policy settings," she said.

"When we talk about the cost of living, we're really talking about an individual household and what pressures they're facing in their day-to-day lives — so to get a sense of that you have to look at the individual consumption basket."

To calculate the CPI, the ABS collects prices for items grouped into 87 categories and 11 groups. Every month, the ABS calculates the price changes of each item from the previous month and aggregates them to work out the inflation rate for the basket.

Prices are collected from a variety of retailers across the eight capital cities and the ABS uses methods like web-scraping and online and telephone interviews with retailers.

A knitter and an EV owner, McCririck said her basket would differ from the "average household's basket".

"But the weights that we give to the basket for the CPI are based on the average household experience," she said.

How are CPI items and weights chosen?

In deciding which goods and services to include in the CPI basket and what their weights should be, the ABS uses data about how much – and on what – households in Australia spend their income.

If households spend more of their income on one item, that item will have a larger weight in the CPI.

McCririck said reweights are based on the ABS' household expenditure survey.

"We've grown forward the CPI weights by looking ... at how trends in the household expenditure change — we've grown the weight forward each year manually," she said.

Looking at the reweight in 2025, the weight for alcohol and tobacco fell because sales of legal tobacco had fallen as smoking rates decline, although it did not include vapes and illicit tobacco.

The weight for housing also fell because home buying declined amid a shortage in new construction and supply. Dwelling commencements in 2024 were the lowest in over ten years.

In 2024, school fees rose in 2024 and there were more non-government school enrolments forcing the weight for education to go up for 2025.

Due to the rise in airfares, Australian household spending on overseas holidays rose so the weight for international holiday travel and accommodation increased.

Inflationary pressures are 'going to persist'

Regardless of the weights, Asher told SBS News that rising inflation is a trend that is likely to continue.

"The wars will continue, which means that fuel prices will continue to be high and that has a flow-on effect on goods, logistics and transport systems — which flows onto anything that's imported," she said.

"Many materials, even if they are locally produced here, will increase."

She said inflationary pressures have seen Australians reduce their spending — a habit she hopes can continue into the Christmas period.

"As we move into the Christmas period, people are worse off now than they were at the beginning of the year with inflation — wage growth hasn't kept up," Asher said.

"Some people will be inclined to still spend at Christmas because they feel obliged to do so. I really think that people should be okay to pull back and not overdo it or put things on credit.

"As we move into next year, it's still going to be incredibly tough. Many of the challenges we're seeing are going to persist."

After a frustrating period of delays that saw just five holes drilled in six weeks, Gateway Mining has put its foot on the accelerator, unleashing a five-rig exploration blitz at its flagship Yandal gold project in Western Australia. The aggressive ramp-up comes as gold remains near historically elevated levels, with the Australian Government forecasting prices to stay high through 2026 and 2027. The broader WA exploration sector is also running hot, with spending in the State hitting a record $843.6 million in the June quarter, creating intense competition for drilling contractors and equipment. The landscape at Gateway Mining’s Yandal gold project in Western Australia’s richly endowed goldfields, where a major exploration campaign is underway. That backdrop may help explain the operational headwinds the company faced following its major Cowza discovery in September; however, Gateway says its exploration program is now fully back on track. With two reverse-circulation (RC) rigs, one diamond rig and one aircore rig now humming on site and a second diamond rig expected to arrive later this week, the company appears to be making up for lost time. Management says it’s on to its third RC drilling contractor, with the new outfit hitting its stride and the two rigs punching out a combined average of 300 metres per day. The RC rigs are focused on following up mineralisation along the highly prospective Cowza-Celia South trend.

Advertisement

‘We are confident we now have the exploration program fully back on track.’ Gateway Mining chief executive officer Richard Pugh Meanwhile, the first of two diamond rigs has kicked off drilling at Cowza, tasked with twinning the original discovery hole. That hole returned a spectacular intercept of 41 metres grading two grams per tonne (g/t) gold, featuring a richer nine-metre core assaying a hefty 7.5g/t gold. Twinning the hole with a diamond core will provide crucial geological data on the orientation of the gold-bearing vein structures, helping guide the ongoing RC drill-out. Once the second diamond rig arrives on site, it will be put to work, testing for extensions to the current mineral resources at the nearby Horse Well deposit. Rounding out Gateway’s comprehensive program, an aircore rig has been brought back to drill a suite of pipeline targets, mostly focused on splay structures branching off the major regional Celia Shear zone. Notably, the company remains well-funded to undertake the extensive campaign, reporting a healthy $52.8 million in its war chest at the end of the September quarter.

Advertisement

Gateway Mining chief executive officer Richard Pugh said: “It has been a frustrating period for Gateway trying to source appropriate drilling contractors who can handle the ground conditions and maintain appropriate daily metreage rates. Only five holes were successfully completed in the six weeks following the discovery announcement at Cowza. We are now onto our third RC contractor, and very pleasingly we are achieving normal drilling rates -over 300 metres per day between the two rigs, on average.” Gateway’s Yandal project sits in the seriously well-endowed gold and regional-scale Yandal greenstone belt. The area hosts a treasure trove of multi-million-ounce gold deposits, including the nearby Jundee, Bronzewing and Darlot mines. Yandal already holds a global gold inventory of 400,400 ounces. Running through Gateway’s patch is the gold-bearing Celia shear, a major geological structure linking a string of the company’s prospects and deposits. Among them are the Dusk ’til Dawn gold camp, boasting 108,900 ounces and the Horse Well gold camp with 291,500 ounces. The shift to a multi-rig program follows a recent board reshuffle that saw chief executive officer Richard Pugh elevated to managing director, sharpening Gateway’s focus on exploration-led growth. Under Pugh’s leadership, the company has delivered multiple discoveries including Haflinger, Hummer, Rubicon and the recent high-grade find at Cowza. Further drilling success could add serious ounces to its golden tally, potentially setting the stage for a resource upgrade next year. With a recently restructured board, a formidable cash war chest and a fleet of five rigs now set to spin the rods around the clock, Gateway appears to have put its operational frustrations firmly in the rear-view mirror. After a quiet spell on the news front, Gateway appears poised to unleash a torrent of assay results as it looks to build on its existing 400,400-ounce gold inventory and pursue its ambition of creating Australia’s next multi-million-ounce gold camp. title: He used to ride bulls. Now he takes calls from the King and has seven Cup runners
text:

Don’t let leading horse trainer Ciaron Maher’s laid-back demeanour be your lasting impression. His mind is like a steel trap. Asked whether he recalled a horse called Electric Turban, he did not miss a beat. “Yeah, that was one of Richard Freyer’s,” Maher said. It is also the most recent horse he rode around the two miles at Flemington, where he will race seven horses on Tuesday in the Melbourne Cup. Loading That ride happened way back in April 2002 when Maher was a tearaway jumps jockey who had moved from Warrnambool to live at the end of the Flemington straight with a bunch of other aspiring jockeys. Maher finished fourth on Electric Turban midway through his career in the saddle that was never going to go far given his size. He rode a respectable 26 winners from 210 rides and finished third in the Brierly Steeplechase at Warrnambool on Yallah Limit in 2002.

Advertisement

“Safe to say that I was better on the other side of the fence,” Maher said. But he recalls with fondness the vibe among jumps jockeys on Melbourne Cup Day as the lesser lights raced in the Cup Hurdle, which was won and done before midday, allowing them to settle in for a big day with family and friends. His only ride in the Cup Hurdle came 26 years ago on Taylors Bridge for the late Peter Hayes. Maher’s mount sat back in the field and just managed to avoid a fallen horse, Gilligan, and finished seventh. Later that day Brew won the big one from the outside barrier. Was he a mad bugger in those days? It’s a reputation the rest of the jumps jockey fraternity used to wear as a badge of honour. ”Some would say I still am,” he said with a wry grin. Despite the pressure of expectation a smile never seems far from Ciaron Maher’s face. Getty Images He hides the madness well, running the country’s biggest training operation with a calmness that seems to translate to his horses. His business has about 900 horses and operates out of six locations – three in Victoria and three in NSW.

Advertisement

The systems and planning required is astounding. Maher invests heavily in science, data analysis and horse wellbeing. What puts Maher among the elite trainers, however, is not the whizz bang devices or the high-performance staff. It’s his desire to learn about horses, which has not diminished from the moment his mum, Eileen, dropped him off at trainer Shayne Fisher’s property near the family dairy farm in Winslow, in Victoria’s south-west, when he was just out of primary school. Fisher, a hugely respected horseman around Warrnambool, laughs at the memories of a bunch of local kids including Ciaron and his brother Declan, his own stepson, Australian equestrian champion Jamie Kermond, and others hanging out at his property on weeknights. On weekends, they would jump in his truck to attend showjumping, pony club events or shetland steeplechase races. “He spent a lot of time at our place,” Fisher recalled. “He was very keen and wanted to have a go at everything. They were wild buggers, got into bull riding and all sorts of things. They weren’t just little kids sitting on the sidelines.

Advertisement

Ciaron Maher and then co-trainer David Eustace won the Melbourne Cup in 2022 with Gold Trip. Jason South “They got to learn the basics with every horse, not just horseracing. We taught them the basics of horse handling,” Fisher said. They became tough, too. Fisher laughed as he recalled Maher one day squealing that he could not stop a horse he was riding only to be told, “point him at the shed”. That, apparently, would encourage the horse to pull up. Maher became an apprentice, before moving to the city to work with the Hayes stable. However, once he turned his attention to training in late 2005, Fisher realised the youngster’s aspirations in that field exceeded his own. Maher didn’t just want to be a trainer, he wanted to be Victoria’s leading trainer. Maher hadn’t wasted his time as a jumps jockey. That speciality requires riders to work with the animal rather than just jumping on their back, often breaking or pre-training horses or doing trackwork. Former jumps jockeys trained the winners of both the Caulfield Cup and Cox Plate this year.

Advertisement

“Normally the jumps jocks are riding the difficult horses,” Maher said. “That [time] was phenomenal for me.” As a track rider he worked for greats such as Bart Cummings, Jim Houlahan and Paddy Payne. He then rode in Ireland and, later, worked there as well, storing the lessons every moment provided. “I never took notes, but I do think about every little thing [I experienced] when a scenario comes up [now],” Maher said. Maher’s first breakthrough as a trainer came when, on the final day of the 2007 Flemington carnival, the gelding Tears I Cry won the group 1 mile at huge odds. He had only been a trainer for two years and after spending time preparing horses out of his parents’ dairy farm in Warrnambool, he moved into two boxes at Caulfield alongside racing greats such as Peter Moody, Mick Price and Rick Hore-Lacey. He had been told if he stayed near home, all he could hope to train were broken-down types from owners hoping for a miracle. His mum thought he would be back in Warrnambool in no time, but he settled in with the experienced crew working their horses there and expanded his operation, winning the 2016 Caulfield Cup with Jameka.

When he was serving jail time in 2024, the crypto exchange billionaire Changpeng Zhao wrote a book with a modest title: Freedom of Money: A Memoir of Protecting Users, Resilience, and the Founding of Binance. The tome was short on introspection. A $US50 million ($71.2 million) personal fine, $US4.3 billion company penalty and four-month stretch in prison for failing to run an effective anti-money laundering scheme were like water off a duck’s back. Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao needs other cryptocurrency exchanges to block suspicious transactions. Bloomberg In one irony-free observation, Zhao wrote of being in jail that “the entire process was designed to deliver the lowest possible customer satisfaction.” The book did little too to explain how Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, has protected its users, except where that is a byproduct of its own rapid growth. Since last Friday, when hackers stole $US6.3 billion in tokens from his website, Zhao has had a chance to turn his words into reality.

Advertisement

If Binance’s announcements since the hack are to be believed, the former chief executive has done a good job of compensating, if not protecting, his users. After a feverish weekend of work, Binance announced on Monday that it had covered 95 per cent of the stolen tokens by value through its unfortunately named SAFU – Security Asset Fund for Users – program and resumed withdrawals. Related Article Cryptocurrencies Inside the scramble to contain the largest crypto heist in history That may turn out to be the easy part. If Binance is to actually get back the billions in tokens that were stolen, Zhao will have to hope that other cryptocurrency companies have better anti-money laundering processes than his firm once did. According to the FBI, the heist was likely carried out by a North Korean hacking group known as TraderTraitor. Early indications suggest that once the hackers started moving tokens, the entire $US6.3 billion was pulled out within half an hour. At that point, much of the haul was in stablecoins such as Tether and Circle, which are designed to track the price of another asset, such as the US dollar. But the hackers rapidly started exchanging those tokens for truly decentralised alternatives, such as Bitcoin and Ethereum. The difference is that Tether and Circle can be frozen by the tech companies that created them; Bitcoin and Ethereum are the wild west.

Advertisement

The cryptocurrency tracking company Chainalysis noted that about half of the stolen coins were frozen by law enforcement and industry players before that could happen. That has put all eyes on the remaining $US3.3 billion worth of coins, which are now pinging between different cryptocurrency platforms, wallets and coins as the hackers try to avoid the watching eyes of law enforcement and crypto analysis companies. Their likely end goal? Convert the money into traditional currency, such as US dollars or Chinese yuan, that the North Korean regime can actually use. Cryptocurrency thefts are perfect for that purpose. Where a traditional hack – and North Korea has executed several, including the Wannacry breach that hit the UK’s National Health Service or the 2014 Sony Pictures attack – might result in the release of sensitive data, mass disruption or a ransom payment in the millions, targeting a big crypto exchange can net billions. In his book, Zhao frames his jail time as a disproportionate punishment for a minor record keeping issue. The US government disagreed, arguing in court that Binance had failed to stop hundreds of millions of dollars in unlawful transactions, including for sanctioned Iranian entities and drug traffickers. Zhao has since been pardoned by US President Donald Trump. He may have moved on, but to stop Binance users’ stolen funds being swapped for traditional money, Zhao needs other cryptocurrency exchanges to do much better at detecting malicious users than Binance did – at least in the past. title: I’ve been to an Ivy League college – our universities are failing at one vital job

NationalUniversity Opinion I’ve been to an Ivy League college – our universities are failing at one vital job Allegra Schubert University student November 2, 2026 — 3:35pm

November 2, 2026 — 3:35pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I returned from my exchange at the University of Pennsylvania with no fewer than 10 T-shirts and jumpers, an assortment of posters and pins, a mug, several tote bags and, much to my surprise, Penn-branded socks. I went to Philadelphia halfway through a five-and-a-half-year degree at the University of Sydney, wanting more than a reprieve from the routine. I returned with something less portable than merchandise: a nagging suspicion that Australian universities are failing to prepare us for life after graduation. Allegra Schubert (pictured right) studies at Sydney University but went to the University of Pennsylvania on exchange. Let me dispel one myth early. The content was not harder. My subjects were pitched at roughly the same level as their USyd equivalents and assessed in much the same way, with a similar weekly workload. If you were hoping for a tale of Ivy League rigour flattening a hapless Australian, I can’t oblige. What differed was the delivery. My professors wrote everything by hand on a blackboard, working through each problem in real time. At home, lecturers often display pre-typed solutions and narrate over them, which is efficient but, I find, ultimately detrimental to the learning experience. Penn’s lectures weren’t compulsory, but they weren’t recorded either. Miss one and your sole recourse was a friend’s notes, so attendance became self-enforcing. Small weekly homework tasks, worth only a few per cent of the grade, obliged me to consolidate each week’s material instead of exhuming it in the final fortnight.

Advertisement

Then there was the cold calling. In classes small enough to allow it, everyone was called on once or twice a session. At USyd, a participation mark can usually be secured with one perfunctory comment, after which you are free to drift off. For someone who had never voluntarily raised a hand in an Australian lecture, this was petrifying. It was also where I learnt the most because I spent every minute knowing I might be next on the chopping block. Related Article Editorial

University Falling university rankings suggest a wider malaise The Herald's View Editorial By the end of semester, my professors knew almost every student by name. At USyd, that relationship is largely outsourced to tutors, usually postgraduate students and, in my early years, undergraduates barely older than me. The biggest difference of all were the students. Every American I met could articulate precisely why they were doing their degree and where it would take them. Second-year students outlined career trajectories that ran, without apparent irony, all the way to retirement. They also asked questions. Constantly. They volunteered answers with no fear of being wrong and posed silly questions without a flicker of embarrassment. Australian lecture theatres, in my experience, are very different. They typically play out as follows: the lecturer pleads for a response, endures a long silence, then supplies the answer themselves. Tall poppy syndrome, as far as I could tell, had not been granted a visa.

Advertisement

This was the part that unsettled me. Three years into a dual degree, I was not sure where it was leading, and neither are most of my Australian university friends. I don’t think my American classmates are any more intelligent than us. They had simply been asked, much earlier and much more insistently, what they wanted to do with their lives. Related Article Education ‘Wake-up call’ as Australian universities slip in world rankings For high-demand courses, an Australian teenager’s future hinges on a few weeks of exams in Year 12, distilled into a single number. American students carry that pressure across years of grades, testing, sport and side projects, and are nudged from the start of high school to work out what genuinely interests them. I am a case study in what happens without that nudge. My ATAR, not my ambition, chose my degree. Like many of my friends, I was backed into a corner by a number. The American approach, to be clear, is no utopia. It favours families who can pay for private tutoring and admissions consultants. Still, it makes teenagers confront a question that we put off for half a decade.

Advertisement

Another difference is how American universities compete for enrolments. The top universities chase the same students by focusing on the experience. Some campuses have gone as far as building lazy rivers; at Penn, faculties hosted dinners, the Dean threw a formal, and societies handed out doughnuts and sodas by the armful. My sock drawer, I now realise, was a line item in a marketing budget. Related Article Opinion

High school If your child starts year 12 exams today, don’t do what I did Margot Saville Deputy opinion editor Australia’s roughly 40 universities are almost all public, large and broadly comparable, and with domestic fees regulated, their fiercest contest is for international students. The domestic student experience is largely overlooked. The 2025 Student Experience Survey found that only 37.3 per cent of domestic undergraduates enrolled on campus attended all their classes in person. Of those, 54.4 per cent felt a sense of belonging, compared with 45.5 per cent of students who mixed online and in-person classes. I’m not suggesting Australia import the American system, price tag and inequity included. But much of what made Penn’s classrooms work would cost very little here. Lecturers could work through problems by hand and cold call in classes small enough to allow it. The people who set the exam could learn the names of the people sitting it. If high school is too late to fix, universities must pick up the slack. In Australia, the name on your testamur rarely sets you apart. What distinguishes a graduate is what they did beyond the syllabus: the project they built, the team they played in, the society they ran. Universities should push students towards these from first year. Most of us, after all, are here to land a career and an income that can support the life we want to live.

Advertisement

Penn won me over with socks. Australian universities, I’m asking you for something worth far more: graduates who walk out knowing what they want to do next and how to achieve it. Allegra Schubert is studying Commerce/Engineering at the University of Sydney.

The changing of the guard at the NRL continues, with premiership winner and former Test centre Mark Gasnier brought in by executive chairman Peter V’landys. The 45-year-old, the bearer of one of the most famous surnames in the game’s history, is understood to have been hired in a senior role with a focus on driving participation. Steve Christo Gasnier retired in 2011, the year after winning a drought-breaking title with St George Illawarra, and later developed Tri Tag Rugby, a non-contact variation of rugby union, and licensed it to Rugby Australia. But the former cross-code star is the latest recruitment of the V’landys era following an exodus of executives from the governing body’s head office at Moore Park. Mark Gasnier during his playing days with the NSW Blues in 2011. title: Cape Town was the batting collapse we had to have. Now selectors must make changes
text:
Advertisement

SportCricketTest cricket Opinion Cape Town was the batting collapse we had to have. Now selectors must make changes Greg Chappell Former Australian Test captain November 2, 2026 — 3:30pm

November 2, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Paul Keating called the early-1990s economic downturn “the recession we had to have.” Similarly, Australia’s 111 in the fourth innings at Newlands was the collapse we had to have. Whether anyone learns from it is another matter. I disagree with Pat Cummins that this is a very good side. It has been an excellent bowling side for a long time, but even the bowlers failed to trouble South Africa at crucial times. The Proteas batters had a plan in the second innings to let the short balls go and make the Australians bowl to them. Simon Harmer bowled South Africa to victory over Australia in Cape Town. AP Photo/Halden Krog It was hard to discern any plan from our batters in their second innings in Cape Town. The Australian batting hasn’t carried its weight for some time, and a team holding a substantial first-innings lead doesn’t fold for 111 in the second innings if the batting is sound. The scoreboard doesn’t lie. I take no pleasure in saying so. I’ve been a batsman, captain, selector and coach, and I’d rather be building than knocking.

Advertisement

I sat in a few dressing rooms after humbling experiences, but with straight shooters like Ian Chappell, Keith Stackpole and Rod Marsh, we were never allowed to pretend that we were just unlucky. It was shape up, or ship out. Pat sees talent and good intent in that room, and he’s right. But to some extent a team operates in a bubble, and inside it every failure is bad luck. From outside, it looks different. Loading Start with the toss. Plenty thought bowling first on a good Cape Town pitch was a mistake, and I suspect Kagiso Rabada running through our top order was the biggest factor. Then we batted last on a surface that has historically helped spin late. A self-inflicted double whammy. We beat South Africa without Rabada in Durban, and that flattered us. But the toss is the least of it.

Advertisement

For years the selectors have patched the batting with experienced first-class players who look reliable on paper. The result is a middle order heavy with age and short on resilience. The names of Michael Hussey and Adam Gilchrist are often trotted out in defence of this approach. Hussey made mountains of runs for Western Australia and would have played much earlier if he hadn’t been stuck behind one of the best line-ups ever. Gilchrist went across the Nullarbor because NSW wouldn’t give him a regular game. Both were blocked, and both were once-in-a-generation players. You can’t build a selection policy on them. Pat Cummins bats on day five. AP Photo/Halden Krog The states aren’t blameless. Sheffield Shield sides pick safe experience over potential, so the national panel is choosing from a pool shaped by caution. Matt Renshaw’s 369 runs at 61.5 was the best news of the tour, and he muddies my argument. He first played for Australia at the age of 20, making 184 against Pakistan at the SCG, then got dropped three times. It was nine years before he made his second hundred. Patience works, say the defenders of the status quo.

Advertisement

I don’t buy it. Renshaw was never a journeyman. We threw away a talent and then had to look for it again. In Durban, we were 4-84 when he came in, and he made 190 off 397 balls. He faced 115 balls on the first day for three boundaries, reached 50 off the second ball of the second morning and put on 134 for the ninth wicket with Nathan Lyon. Matt Renshaw should open the batting for Australia. Getty Images He left well and hit anything straight. A bouncer found his grille, and he just carried on. His words afterwards told you what the chance meant to him. I lost my place in the Test team early in my career and wondered if I really belonged. It was only for a few weeks, so I can’t imagine what it must feel like to be on the outside for most of a decade. Renshaw is 30 now, and he’s back because the selectors ran out of options, not because anyone had a plan. Imagine what we’d have if we’d kept faith with him in 2017 and let him grow inside the side. That’s the lesson of his story.

Advertisement

It also settles the question that’s bugged the selectors since David Warner retired. Renshaw leaves the ball well, is hard to shift, and he sees off the new ball. He batted at five in Durban, but his game is built for the top of the order. Renshaw opens. Selector must put Marnus Labuschagne out of his misery. Getty Images The identity of his partner is the next problem. Travis Head thrives at home, where pace and bounce suit him down to the ground. On lower, slower pitches overseas, his slashing game gets exposed. He is caught in the infield or drags on to his stumps. I’m not convinced he’s an opener away from Australia. Cameron Green looks better since his injury, but his early footwork worries me. He’s so intent on survival that he takes short strides to full balls, which leaves his contact point well in front of his eyes. The hands get pushed out, the face opens, and there’s a gap between bat and pad. Against spin, it’s worse: short strides leave you short of the pitch of the ball, and the hands have too much to do. He needs a longer first stride, with the contact point under his eyes. Running down the pitch to defend against a spinner is a sure way to promote short strides.

Advertisement

I experienced similar problems at various times in my career and made a conscious effort to exaggerate my footwork in net sessions to train a longer forward stride. Cam has enormous levers, but he is not using them. He must smother the seam movement and spin, or he won’t be the player he could be. Josh Inglis wants to score, not survive. Green ran him out in the second innings, but Inglis has done enough for at least another series. Then there is Marnus Labuschagne. The selectors cannot dodge it any longer. I call it elite performance decline: the older player starts to doubt himself. Steve Waugh admitted that late in his career the mental effort outweighed the joy. I think Marnus is there. The kindest thing the selectors can do is put him out of his misery. Drop him for the summer and send him back to domestic cricket. Ban the video analysis too. He’s spent years studying himself when he should be watching the ball. Strip away the triggers, guard changes and endless tinkering, and let him go back to hitting it. Looking ahead, I’d make Cricket Australia do something about the states. Tie funding and academy resources to debuting and developing young players in the top four. Then look at Oliver Davies, who wants to score and puts the bowler under pressure. Look at Sam Konstas, with his classical high-elbow technique. Look at Campbell Kellaway, who has the desire to occupy the crease all day.

Advertisement

Related Article Australian cricket Coach calls for calm, keeps door ajar for Labuschagne, as Healy turns torch on selectors The selectors will be back at the drawing board for New Zealand, but those conditions will be familiar and suit our pace attack, which covers a lot of cracks. India is a different story. Turning pitches blunt the quicks and expose a fragile batting line-up. The road back to the Test final is full of potholes. Newlands wasn’t only about talent. It was about a system afraid of risk, one that papers over cracks with domestic veterans while first-class cricket decays into a white-ball shadow. If Cricket Australia and the states hide behind platitudes, the home summer will be harder than it needs to be. If they take the shock, this can be the correction that sets us right. title: Dees sweat on injury ahead of blockbuster AFLW final; Freo turn to Wharfie Time … but fail to score
text:
Sydney have confirmed their home AFLW elimination final against the Western Bulldogs after overcoming Wharfie Time and a horror injury to beat Fremantle by one point.

Play was held up for 10 minutes in the first quarter on Sunday at Cockburn before Swans ruck Caitlin Reid was stretchered from the field. She was felled by a clash of heads with Fremantle’s Hayley Miller.

After Sydney rallied in the second half and took the lead, Miller snapped a goal to bring the Dockers to within one point and Wharfie Time was sounded, with less than 90 seconds on the clock.

But just as the crowd activation backfired horribly in the AFL grand final loss to Brisbane, the Dockers could not score again.

Chloe Molloy took a game-saving mark with 15 seconds left and the Swans won 5.7 (37) to 5.6 (36), denying Dockers star Ash Brazill a farewell win.

Molloy kicked four goals to break the AFLW goalkicking record with 28, two up on Hawthorn’s Aine McDonagh and Geelong forward Jackie Perry. Sydney racked up nine wins, a club record.

“It’s a good catapult ... into the finals, close wins like that,” Molloy told Fox Footy.

“It always brings out a bit extra energy, especially when you hear Wharfie Time.”

Geelong will host Melbourne, followed by reigning premiers North Melbourne against Carlton in a qualifying-final double header next Saturday afternoon at Ikon Park.

Sydney expect to pack out Henson Park on Sunday against the Bulldogs, before Gold Coast host Hawthorn in the other elimination final.

title: Airport rail study doctored to ‘bake-in’ Sunshine as preferred route, commission told
text:

Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election Airport rail study doctored to ‘bake-in’ Sunshine as preferred route, commission told Chip Le Grand Updated November 2, 2026 — 3:03pm ,first published November 2, 2026 — 5:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. State Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has urged the Big Build royal commission to fully investigate allegations that former premier Jacinta Allan coerced public servants to back her government’s plans for the Melbourne Airport Rail Project. But Wilson said that if the Coalition government is elected, the project would continue as designed. Jacinta Allan, pictured next to Daniel Andrews, announces Sunshine as the preferred route for the Melbourne Airport Rail Link before the 2018 election. Paul Jeffers This masthead on Monday reported allegations before the royal commission that financial estimates were doctored, and a senior public servant was threatened with the sack to ensure the proposed MARL ran through Sunshine instead of a more direct route to the city. The allegations challenge the integrity of the business case for Premier Ben Carroll’s priority project, call into question a $12 billion joint funding commitment by the state and federal governments, and plunge the Big Build into fresh scandal a month before the state election.

Advertisement

Related Article Victorian election Wilson insists SRL position is ‘very clear’ despite days of confusion Wilson said the royal commission needed to examine the claims. “What we need to get to the bottom of is how, eight years ago, a minister – Jacinta Allan at the time – was intimidating, bullying and threatening public servants to get a political outcome,” she said on Monday. “That is what the royal commission needs to look into.” Pressed on whether a Coalition government would review the project in light of the allegations or consider an alternative route, Wilson said it would be built as planned. “The route is the route. The contracts have been signed, the project is underway and the Coalition is committed to delivering airport rail.”

Advertisement

Allan denies the allegations. She is expected to be called as a witness before the commission. A confidential submission to the royal commission by a planning expert who advised on the airport rail link reveals that a secret working group was established in late 2017 or early 2018 at the direction of then-public transport minister Allan to allegedly bake in the case for the Sunshine route. It says the small group, which included public servants within the Transport Department and outside consultants, was told to not discuss its work with any of their colleagues, including direct reports, or diarise their meetings. All instructions were given verbally. The group’s brief, according to the submission, was to study four shortlisted routes for the Melbourne Airport Rail Link (MARL) and build evidence supporting the state government’s politically favoured outcome – that the new train line, if ever built, would have to go through Sunshine.

Advertisement

“The task was to produce a document, or set of documents, prior to the 2018 election so that after that election there would be no further consideration of any alternative routes for the MARL other than through Sunshine,” the submission reads. Carroll did not address the allegations before the royal commission when questioned by this masthead. On Monday, he cancelled a pre-scheduled press conference. Premier Ben Carroll axed a pre-scheduled press conference on Monday. Louis Trerise “The premier’s first act was to establish the toughest royal commission into the construction industry to leave no stone unturned,” a spokesman said on Sunday. “The terms of reference are broad and expansive. Nothing is off limits. We won’t pre-empt its findings.” Opposition transport infrastructure spokesman Evan Mulholland said Victorians were owed a more substantial response. “Ben Carroll was sitting around the table as a deputy premier and as a senior minister in the government. He needs to explain what he knew and when he knew it.”

Advertisement

The submission from the planing expert is one of four to the royal commission raising concerns about the integrity of the current MARL project. All were provided to this masthead by their respective authors. The most serious allegation raised by the planning expert is that, to make an iron-clad case for Sunshine, the estimated cost of a more direct route through Maribyrnong was intentionally inflated by exaggerating the amount of tunnelling required. And the winner is – Sunshine. The state government announced its preferred route in 2018. Paul Jeffers The Maribyrnong route would have run beneath Highpoint shopping centre and opened up disused defence land for residential development. An earlier 2012 study, commissioned by the then Liberal state government, top-scored Maribyrnong, known at the time as the “direct tunnel” option, out of 22 possible routes, with Sunshine ranked a close second.

Advertisement

The allegation that costings were deliberately inflated to rule Maribyrnong out of contention is contained in a separate, contemporaneous file note made by a solicitor when the planning expert first sought legal advice about blowing the whistle. The note, dated August 23, 2018, and seen by The Age, reads: “Untenable. Serious matters ignored, not acted upon. “4 options – one particular route better but more expensive (doctored to make it unviable).” The solicitor who wrote the file note confirmed its authenticity. The planning expert, who spoke to this masthead on the condition of anonymity, decided against making a disclosure to the Victorian Ombudsman or IBAC due to fears of personal and professional recriminations. They subsequently quit the department, leaving the information buried for eight years.

Advertisement

“This is fraud on a billion-dollar scale,” they said. The planning expert, working with trusted former colleagues experienced in rail engineering and major project costing, has calculated that an unnecessary 3.5 kilometres of tunnelling was included along the proposed Maribyrnong route to add between $3.8 billion and $4.6 billion to the estimated cost. A price tag of $20 billion to $25 billion for Maribyrnong – double the estimated $8 billion to $13 billion cost of the Sunshine route – was included in a strategic appraisal of the airport rail link published by Transport for Victoria in July 2018 and built into the 2021 business case for the project. A truer, average cost estimate of the Maribyrnong route, according to detailed calculations provided to this masthead by the group of experts, is $16.5 billion in 2018 dollars.

Advertisement

Maribyrnong was the federal government’s preferred route when then-prime minister Malcolm Turnbull came to Melbourne in April 2018 to announce $5 billion in funding towards the project. Related Article Public service Thrown in a loop: How Daniel Andrews’ biggest project was cooked up behind closed doors Then-premier Daniel Andrews, who did not appear at the funding announcement alongside Turnbull, was blindsided by the move. At the time, he was more focused on his government’s plans to unveil the Suburban Rail Loop, a project being developed in secret, as a vote-grabbing election promise. The Victorian government formally endorsed the Sunshine route for the airport rail link in August 2018 and the federal government followed suit three months later. The comparative cost of the Maribyrnong route was a critical factor in tipping the scales towards Sunshine in the published assessment. According to the Transport for Victoria analysis, Maribyrnong was the top-scoring route for the benefits it would bring to travellers using the line, Victorian businesses and the economic development of Melbourne’s inner north-west. Due to its prohibitive cost, it was ranked last for deliverability.

Advertisement

When the planning expert saw the assessment, he challenged an executive working in the department. “I just said to him, “How could you produce documents like this, and think this is OK?” the planning expert told this masthead. “He said to me, ‘The minister said to me that either these documents say Sunshine or I’ll sack you. So they say Sunshine.’” Allan, who is retiring from politics after losing the Labor leadership to Carroll in July, was the minister for public transport and major projects at the time the assessment was done. “The allegations made are incorrect,” a spokesman for the former premier said. “Ms Allan will co-operate with the important work of the royal commission. She will answer whatever questions the royal commission has for her about these allegations, but it is not appropriate to pre-empt the royal commission’s work.”

Advertisement

Related Article Analysis

Big Build royal commission Royal commission hints at original sin of Big Build A colleague of Allan, who was unauthorised to publicly discuss the matter, said the former premier was furious at the suggestion she would coerce public servants to support a particular outcome. Allan made no secret during her time as a minister responsible for what became known as the Big Build that she wanted the MARL to run through Sunshine. The benefits of Sunshine, which Allan advocated within government and to her federal counterparts, was that it required no tunnelling, would accelerate Sunshine’s development as a second central business district, and would link the airport line with rail services to regional centres. A former cabinet colleague of Allan’s, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said the former premier was insistent the airport rail line had to run through Sunshine so that people travelling to the airport by train from Ballarat or her home town of Bendigo only needed to change trains once.

Advertisement

In December 2018, when defending the government’s decision not to make public a preliminary business case for the project, Allan hinted at a Sunshine bias. “We’ve released previously ... the strategic assessment of the four alignments, which is really what the preliminary business case was about, looking at those four alignments and giving [state and federal] governments the confidence that Sunshine stacked up the best,” she said. Allan’s confidence in the strategic assessment was not shared by the Victorian Auditor-General’s Office (VAGO). The Big Build royal commission led by Chris Kourakis will begin public hearings next week. Joe Armao A 2022 VAGO report into the quality of government business cases used to support major projects was highly critical of the way that route options for the MARL were assessed, describing the work done as “not sufficiently rigorous” and lacking in transparency. The auditor-general noted that the options assessments “significantly influenced” a state government decision to commit $5 billion to the project and were not “validated or revisited in any depth” before they were included in the published business case.

Advertisement

The airport rail allegations go to the heart of a question that commissioner Chris Kourakis has flagged will be central to his inquiry into the Big Build – whether the state government’s $100 billion infrastructure program was primarily designed to advance the public interest or Labor’s electoral prospects. In his opening address to the inquiry, Kourakis noted that “governments must select and design infrastructure projects around the socioeconomic needs of the Victorian public, and not party political interest”. William McDougall (pictured in 2019) worked on most of the major transport construction projects in Victoria since the late 1990s. Jason South The royal commission is scheduled to hold its first public hearings next week. William McDougall, an independent transport planner who has worked in Britain, the Middle East and on signature Big Build projects including the West Gate Tunnel, North East Link, Suburban Rail Loop and the MARL, has told the commission this is not his experience.

Advertisement

“Throughout my career, I have seen an accelerating shift away from integrated, evidence-based planning towards politically selected and prioritised projects,” he writes in a submission provided to this masthead. “The most egregious issue of all is that large projects are chosen for political reasons, announced and funded without the context of an integrated land use and transport plan.” Premier Ben Carroll, pictured with Anthony Albanese near Sunshine, has declared the MARL his “highest priority”. Jason South McDougall, who is aware of the allegations about the development of the MARL now before the royal commission, believes the project is a case study of where Victoria’s planning for and delivery of major transport projects has gone wrong. “A strategic assessment of options … was used to justify the Sunshine/Albion route, but it was a highly skewed assessment with direct, political interference aimed at ensuring that the Sunshine route was the best,” he writes in his submission. “Faster, shorter and cheaper routes were rejected.”

Advertisement

Two further submissions to the royal commission, both made confidentially by former public servants, question the planning process and decisions taken that resulted in Sunshine being chosen as the route for a new airport line. Carroll, since becoming Labor leader, has declared the airport rail link his “highest priority” major project. The government has selected a preferred bidder to redevelop Sunshine station, and Carroll last month was alongside Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to announce forward plans to lay down airport rail tracks to a proposed new station in Keilor East, in the middle of his electorate of Niddrie. The Victorian Coalition has also backed the MARL. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has promised to deliver the project, including a new station at Keilor East, if she becomes Victoria’s next premier. Both the Maribyrnong and Sunshine routes run through Keilor East. Wilson has promised to expand the royal commission’s terms of reference so that it examines whether “any project was conceived, selected, prioritised, expanded, re-scoped, funded or continued, wholly or partly, to confer an industrial, financial, organisational or political benefit” to a trade union or political party.

Fellow riders back Harry Coffey to take hi ride in Melbourne Cup.

Irish trainer has five Cup runners but no luggage. Trainer Nick Ryan has been stood down and a vet questioned by stewards in a case involving the alleged discovery of syringes in a glove box. Getty Images Two syringes containing darbepoetin alfa were allegedly discovered in Ryan’s car outside his Flemington stable on Saturday morning.

Stewards released a statement on Monday, saying Ryan’s licence to train horses had been suspended effective immediately pending the resumption of their inquiries. They also said separate evidence was taken from equine vet Dr Luke Campbell about his “conduct at the time of Saturday’s stable inspection”. Stewards will continue their inquiries with Ryan and Campbell at a date to be fixed. Horses under Ryan’s care will be transferred to other stables. At Monday’s inquiry, stewards took evidence from Ryan’s legal representative. Stewards accepted documented evidence that Ryan was not able to attend. Stewards adjourned the matter for 28 days after an application by Ryan’s legal representative. Campbell has been contacted for comment. Separately, Racing Victoria (RV) veterinarians on Monday completed their second round of pre-race physical veterinary inspections of all horses in the final field for tomorrow’s $10.2 million Melbourne Cup (3200m) at Flemington. All 24 horses were passed suitable to race.

Jockey Rachel King admires fellow hoop Harry Coffey’s desperate effort to ride Shockletz in the Melbourne Cup after injuring his collarbone in a fall on Saturday and is confident he won’t take the ride unless he knows he can perform at his best. Harry Coffey has the ride on Shockletz in Tuesday’s Melbourne Cup. Getty Images The Sydney-based rider, who is aboard So You Are in the Cup, said Coffey had the support of jockeys as he tried to get his body right for the race. “All credit to him if he can definitely get there by tomorrow,” King said on Monday.

Maher, who trains Shockletz, was prepared to keep the door ajar for Coffey to take the mount, which is considered a strong lightweight chance in the race.

Cup-winning jockey James McDonald said on Monday he understood Coffey’s mindset and his refusal to give up the battle to be fit. Related Article Melbourne Cup He’d just ridden his first group 1 race. Then came the death threats “He’s tougher than most of us,” McDonald said. “It’s like a grand final for us … we get up for anything.” Coffey rode Port Guillaume into 21st place in the 2021 Cup and finished 14th on Grand Promenade in 2022. Michael Dee is on standby to take the mount if Coffey’s bid fails. Pondalowie also rose to her feet and returned to her stable fit and well on Saturday night.

Luggage lost in transit as International trainers arrive to plunder Cups Peter Ryan

Irish trainer Joseph O’Brien is confident his five runners will perform in Tuesday’s Melbourne Cup, but he is not so sure what he will be wearing at Flemington after his luggage was mislaid in transit during his trip from America. Joseph O’Brien runs an eye over horses doing trackwork at Werribee last week. “The market is the market,” O’Brien said. “I find in a race like the Melbourne Cup, and big handicaps in general, it’s the one who gets the perfect trip and things set up for them good on the day that ultimately will matter.” O’Brien is looking to become the youngest trainer from outside Australia to win the race three times having already won Cups with Rekindling in 2017 and Twilight Payment in 2020. Loading He expected his longest shot Kizlyar to improve on his disappointing Moonee Valley Cup run when he finished down the track in a slow race. O’Brien said Geelong Cup winner Point of Law, who Ciaron Maher trains, could not have done any more since he arrived in Australia and deserved to start favourite.

“He beat two smart horses in Small Fry and Omni Man, and he is the one everyone has to beat,” O’Brien said. Boom UK trainer, George Boughey, who also arrived without his luggage on the same flight as O’Brien, said he preferred dry conditions for Hopewell Rock, who has excited track watchers during his time in Australia. Trainer Chris Waller at the Call of the Card function. Eddie Jim He will be ridden by Zac Lloyd and be Boughey’s first Melbourne Cup runner. He was working for Gai Waterhouse in 2013 when Fiorente won the Cup. “His stamina is his forte. He has never run 3200m, but I think it was he is made to do,” Boughey said. “When he didn’t become a Derby horse last year, I earmarked him to come down here.

Accelerate Resources has called in the nation’s top scientific minds, partnering with the government research organisation CSIRO to crack the metallurgical code of its Woodie Woodie North manganese project in Western Australia’s prolific Pilbara region. The company has been awarded a $50,000 Kick-Start research grant, which will fund a detailed characterisation study on its manganese mineralisation – a critical step in designing an effective processing flowsheet and assessing the potential for a saleable product. Large-diameter metallurgical drill core from Accelerate Resources’ Woodie Woodie North project, now at CSIRO’s Perth laboratory for detailed analysis. The study, titled Multiscale Characterisation of Manganese Mineralisation, is to be led by CSIRO’s Dr Yoram Teitler and will analyse 150 metres of large-diameter diamond core from the Dale’s Patch and Nathan’s Flat prospects within the project’s Area 42 deposit. In the first stage, CSIRO will log and scan the core for manganese and associated elements using X-ray fluorescence (XRF) and hyperspectral techniques, while measuring hardness. The second stage will involve petrographic, mineralogical and microanalytical work on representative samples to examine how each mineralisation style formed and how subsequent weathering may have altered their characteristics.

Advertisement

‘CSIRO brings world class mineral characterisation capability to understand how the different manganese ore types behave and give us a much sharper picture of the upgrade potential.’ Accelerate Resources chief executive officer Luke Meter The analysis will help explain how different types of manganese mineralisation respond to processing, while guiding the company’s ongoing metallurgical and ore-sorting testwork. The findings are also expected to sharpen Accelerate’s geological understanding of the deposit, helping inform future resource evaluation and mine planning. Accelerate Resources chief executive officer Luke Meter said: “CSIRO brings world class mineral characterisation capability that would be very difficult for a company of our size to access on this scale. Understanding how the different manganese ore types at Area 42 behave is fundamental to designing the right processing route.” With the core already delivered to CSIRO’s Kensington laboratory in Perth, work is expected to begin shortly. The study is due to finish in mid-2027, when CSIRO will deliver a technical report and recommendations for further work. Accelerate will report its own metallurgical and ore-sorting results as they become available. Woodie Woodie North covers 432 square kilometres, 55km north of Consolidated Minerals’ operating Woodie Woodie manganese mine, in a region known for high-grade manganese. The commodity is on Australia’s Critical Minerals List for its essential role in steelmaking and growing use in lithium-ion battery chemistries.

Advertisement

Accelerate has already defined a maiden inferred resource of 1.2 million tonnes grading a respectable 19.1 per cent manganese and has outlined a much larger conceptual exploration target of between 5.3 million and 10.7 million tonnes at 10 to 19 per cent manganese. Neither includes the company’s Gingarrigan and El Largo trends. These high-grade corridors sit beyond both figures and emerged throughrecent mapping of more than 200 manganese outcrops across Woodie Woodie North. Rock chips returned up to 59.4 per cent manganese at El Largo, 12km south-east of Area 42, and 59.6 per cent at the separate Faris prospect 2km south-east of the resource. The surface grades flag the potential for a simple direct-shipping-ore (DSO) operation down the track, subject to further drilling and metallurgical tests. While drilling is ongoing across the project, the core being studied comes from earlier large-diameter work at Area 42, where Accelerate reported visual manganese across a 72-metre downhole span at Nathan’s Flat in October, from 5.6m to the end of the hole at 77.6m. The CSIRO collaboration adds another dimension to Accelerate’s manganese ambitions at Woodie Woodie North, which sits alongside its gold projects in WA’s Eastern Goldfields at Balagundi and Kanowna East, and lithium prospects near Karratha. For a junior explorer, leveraging CSIRO’s world-class firepower is a serious coup. Getting the metallurgy right is often the key that unlocks a project’s value, and by decoding its ore, Accelerate could be fast-tracking its path from Pilbara explorer to producer. title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
